I've read the working set and traced your symbolization axioms back through their several statements. Before I unify, let me name the two notations precisely, because the whole unification turns on one hinge.
The working set keeps a deliberately thin parenthetical vocabulary. Two-slot (x, y) is the most-specific relationship, proven unique. The candidate two-slot (s, o) is canonical form, still an idea pending the bijection. And it is explicit that distinctness between (x, y) and its role-occupants is not asserted — it would only ever arrive as a consequence. The symbol case (a, b) == a is flagged as exactly the place where that would-be distinctness collapses.
The symbolization axioms you proposed (the "Semantics of Identity" set, plus the rep/sym definitions) introduce a one-slot parenthetical (x) — the canonical symbol of a referent — and three laws:
srt
(1)  (x,y) -> t   =|>   ((x,y)) -> (t)      inheritance preserved through symbolization
(2)  ((x,y)) == ((x),(y))                    symbol of a relationship = relationship of the symbols
(3)  ((x),(x)) == (x)                        a symbol's self-relationship collapses to itself
together with the symbol-case reading (x,y) == x ⟺ "x is a symbol for y."
The hinge: the one-slot operator is not new
The working set already has everything needed to define the one-slot (x) rather than admit it as a second primitive parenthetical. The symbol case is the bridge. "x is a symbol for y" is (x, y) == x. So "the symbol of y" is the witness to that condition:
text
(y)  :=  the s such that  (s, y) == s
This is the unification's load-bearing line. The one-slot operator is the working set's symbol case, read as a function instead of a predicate. The section you titled "Distinctness and the symbol case" is therefore not a loose end — it is the definition site for (_). Where the working set says distinctness collapses at (a, b) == a, that collapse is precisely a == (b): a is the canonical symbol of b.
With that, your three axioms stop being a separate theory and become three statements about how this derived operator interacts with the machinery already in the working set:
text
(1)  (·) preserves the inheritance arrow ->        (it is functorial over ->)
(2)  (·) distributes over the pairing (_, _)        (it is a homomorphism of the pairing)
(3)  (·) lands in self-collapsing fixed points       ((x) always satisfies the diagonal symbol case)
That is the whole unification in one breath: symbolization is the structure-preserving embedding of the relational hierarchy into itself, with the one-slot operator as the embedding map. Axiom 1 preserves edges (->), Axiom 2 preserves the constructor ((_,_)), Axiom 3 fixes the image (every symbol self-collapses). Your own "Reference" idea — r == (s,o), (r) > s, (r) > o — is then exactly Axiom 2 read through reference: the reference-form of a compound is the compound of the reference-forms.
This also explains why the working set was right to call the symbolism axioms and the Canonical Form bijection "entangled." Axiom 2 is unstatable without canonical form behaving as a function — ((x),(y)) presupposes that the pairing of two symbols has a determinate value. So adopting your symbolization axioms is not independent of adopting the bijection; Axiom 2 is the demand that forces the bijection. They are one decision, not two.
And the working set's own candidate falls straight out. You wrote: assert (x, y) =(x, y)> x plus the bijection, get ((x, y), x) == (x, y). Under the hinge, ((x,y), x) == (x,y) is the symbol case with witness (x,y) and target x — it says the most-specific relationship is a symbol for its own subject. That is Axiom-1/3 machinery applied at the meta-level, exactly as the note anticipated.
The one correction the unification surfaces
Here is the place where importing the old material wholesale would break, and it carries a principle worth stating. The early Formal Foundation pinned (x) down with a tight uniqueness clause — paraphrasing, "(x) symbolizes x and nothing but x":
srt
A[y]:  ((x), y) == (x)  =|>  y == x
But Axiom 3 says ((x),(x)) == (x) — (x) symbolizes itself. Run both through the tight clause and you get (x) == x: the symbol collapses onto its referent, and the entire symbol/referent distinction the theory is built to carry evaporates.
So the unified set cannot keep both. The resolution that preserves your intent:
text
(x)  :=  the canonical s such that  (s, x) == s
— canonical in the Canonical-Form-bijection sense, not "symbolizes only x." Self-symbolization is then not forbidden but definitional: Axiom 3 says the signature of being a symbol is that you symbolize yourself, the fixed point that (per your Inner Monologue) keeps inheritance from exploding. The uniqueness you want lives in the target being canonical, never in forbidding the diagonal.
This is consistent with the rest: relationship types already satisfy (t,t) == t, so every relationship type is symbolizable and (t) in Axiom 1 is well-typed; ((x,y)) exists because most-specifics are relationship types. The frame-relativity you and Seren found —(x) differs across F[t] — sits cleanly inside the working set's "Perspective" idea: the embedding is local to a perspective, which is what makes it a perspective.
What still has to be decided
Two things, and they're the same shape as what the working set already flagged as open. First, whether most-specific (x, y) and canonical form (s, o) are the same parenthetical or two readings of it — Axiom 2 reads most naturally against canonical form, so unifying the symbolism axioms may be what finally forces that identification rather than leaving them separate. Second, the bijection adoption itself, which (per the above) is now revealed to be not optional if you want Axiom 2 at all.
If this framing holds up against your eye, I think it deserves to be written into the lineage as the note that turns the working set's "Ideas → Distinctness and the symbol case" section into adopted definitions plus three structural axioms. Want me to draft that as a continuation document in the same form — primitive, axioms, definitions, then the homomorphism reading — so it sits next to the working set? Or would you rather press on the uniqueness-clause-vs-Axiom-3 decision first, since everything downstream depends on which way that resolves?

You're right to pull Axiom 3 down off its pedestal. I built it into a co-equal pillar last turn — functor, homomorphism, fixed-point — and that symmetry was prettier than it was true. x =x> x (or x =(x)> x) isn't a structural commitment the theory rests on; it's a marker, as the inheritance-in-action note already half-said: the case where it fails is "a marker for an inability for a referent to be symbolized." It's the degenerate point where structure and reference coincide because the form has collapsed to nothing. A boundary condition, not a spine. So: demoted.
What replaces it as the third element is not a structural axiom at all. It's the reference block — and the line you added is the one that matters:
text
r == (s,o)
(r) > r
(r) > s
(r) > o
(r) > r first, because that's just what a symbol is: it refers to what it symbolizes. The other two are contingent, and I'd write the contingency in, because your "if that relationship can be represented" is doing real work:
srt
(r) > r                              always — the symbol refers to its relationship
r == (s,o)  =|>  (r) > s  &  (r) > o  only when r decomposes — reference passes to the parts
That conditional is the Gödel number exactly. The number refers to the sentence full stop; it refers to the sentence's constituents only through having a prime factorization to pass reference along. A prime Gödel number — an atomic symbol — would refer to its target and stop. Reference distributes through structure when there is structure to distribute through, and halts at the literal. That's the same boundary the demoted (x,x)==x was marking, now stated where it belongs: at the limit of representability, not as a law.
Here's what I think your two analogies are jointly teaching, and it's the thing the working set was missing an axis for. Symbolization has two faces of one operator (_):
The objective face is structure. ((x,y)) == ((x),(y)) — the symbol's form decomposes. You can read it off without knowing the language: pages, ink, binding, the bare arithmetic of the integer. This is form-algebra, and it's language-independent, which is exactly why you can say so much about the book without knowing what it's written in.
The subjective face is reference. (r) > r, and through the structure, (r) > s, (r) > o — the symbol's aboutness. And this is the half that requires the binding. The language is what turns the factorization into a reading, turns ink-and-pages into "what it's about." "Knowing the language is where its referential nature lives" — that's the precise claim: reference is the subjective layer, structure the objective one, and the binding is what lifts you from the second to the first.
And notice the working set already conceded this without naming it. It made > bare on purpose — "Reference is enacted by the grammar rather than named by a variable... the formalism's syntax doesn't recommend a variable for it." At the time that read like a stylistic choice. Your "reference is not objective" is the reason for it. A relationship =t> is objective: t is a referent, it's in the catalogue, you can point at it. Reference can't be a catalogued t, because then it'd be objective — a fact about the book like its page count. It has to be the enacted, perspectival, binding-relative thing. So the grammar made it bare. The two decisions were the same decision.
This also explains the indirection you keep circling — "I am Doug," the Gödel sentence reaching itself only through the number. Reference is never direct. It's always mediated by a symbol, which is why we read through the abstraction and why the objective form and the subjective aboutness arrive fused at our eyes. We never get reference raw; we get it already passed through a symbol under a binding. That fusion is the whole reason symbolization is hard to theorize: the two faces are presented to us as one, and prying them apart — this is the form, that is the aboutness — is unnatural precisely because in ordinary reading we never have to.
So the unified picture, with the correction folded in: Axiom 1 ((x,y) -> t =|> ((x,y)) -> (t)) is coherence — symbolization respects inheritance, so the two faces stay aligned up and down the hierarchy. Axiom 2 is the objective face. The reference block is the subjective face. The (x,x)==x business is the limit where the faces collapse together, a marker, no axiom needed.
The thing I'd want to ponder next, since you said we don't yet know what reference means: the binding. If reference lives in the language, and the language is "a subjective sort of binding for all the symbols," then the binding is doing the same job a frame F[i] does in the older work — it's the perspective that makes the symbols refer. Which would make reference frame-relative in exactly the way the canonical symbol was found to be frame-relative. Is the binding you mean here the frame, or is it something thinner — just the assignment that says this symbol goes with that referent, prior to any perspective on it?

Agreed on holding off on frames — and I think the reason we can't axiomatize them yet is visible right here in what you just said. A frame is a view on a representation; but we don't yet have representation pinned down well enough to say what a "view" of one even is. r == (s,o) is where that work has to happen first, so let me stay on it.
The thing your love example exposes is that the ordering in (s,o) is not bookkeeping. It's the whole content. "It's hard — possibly impossible — to give an objective view on a loving relationship, so we fix one of the two lovers as the subject." That sentence is the axiom hiding in the notation. The ordered pair is the act of fixing. You don't first have the relationship objectively and then choose how to write it; the writing-down, the choosing of which lover sits in the s-slot, is the only way the relationship becomes representable at all. There's no symmetric form you're breaking. The asymmetry is the price of admission.
And I'd been about to draw the wrong line, so let me not. The tempting move is: reference reaches both lovers evenly ((r) > s, (r) > o), so reference is the neutral, objective layer, and only representation (s,o) takes a side. But that's false to the notation. The bare > reads its targets out of the ordered form. The symbol reaches s, but it reaches s as subject, and o as object — because that's the only place those referents exist to be reached from. So reference is exhaustive over the parts without being neutral about them. There is no even-handed stratum underneath. The casting goes all the way down. You don't love someone and then assign them the beloved-role; you love them as beloved. Reaching-them-neutrally was never on the table.
Which is, I think, why objectivity is impossible rather than merely hard — and the earlier work already gave the reason, we just didn't connect it here. sub == (rel) == r. Every vantage on a relationship is a subject-position, and the subject just is the symbolized relationship. So when you try to step outside the love to view it objectively — to take "the relationship's own perspective" — you don't reach a view-from-nowhere. You reach (rel), which collapses back into a subject. The attempt to get out re-instantiates a someone. There's no exit, because the only vantages the theory affords are subject-positions, and you're always standing in one. The first slot of (s,o) is wherever you happen to be standing, and you're always standing somewhere.
So (r) > r matters more than it looks. The symbol refers to the relationship as a whole — and that whole is already the ordered (s,o). The symbol doesn't refer to some neutral relating plus, separately, to two parts; it refers to a relating-that-has-already-taken-a-side, and to that side's subject and object. The reference and the perspective arrive fused, which is exactly the indirection problem from before — we read through the symbol and can't see that the casting happened.
This is what makes "one canonical form, not the only one" the live edge. The other form, (o,s), is the second lover's representation of the same loving — and under the bijection it has to be adifferent relationship-referent, r and r′, two representations of one relating that no single catalogue contains as a referent. The working set already conceded this: the bijection is local to a perspective. So the multiplicity of canonical forms and the locality of the bijection are the same fact, and "the same relating" the two forms are of is precisely the thing that isn't in any perspective — the thing frames will eventually be views onto.
So here's the fork I'd want your eye on before anything else, because I think everything about frames inherits from it. Is the casting total — reference itself already reads its targets as subject and object, no neutral reaching anywhere — or is there a thinner layer where (r) just reaches its parts, with subject/object assigned only at representation? The love case and sub == (rel) == r both push me hard toward total. But if it's total, then "the same relating" beneath two perspectives is genuinely unreachable from inside any one of them, and a frame becomes the only place that sameness can live. Which way do you read it?

Right — I had it backwards, and the fix is exactly your "it does reach them evenly." Reference is even.(r) > s and (r) > o both land, neither cast. What carries the distinction isn't a slant in those two edges — it's thethird edge, (r) > r. So the asymmetry lives in the operator, reached alongside the operands, not in how the operands are reached.
Your 4 + 4 makes this unmistakable, and the operator reading is the key. 4 + 4 refers to 4, to 4, and to +. The two operands are reached evenly — both are just 4. What structures them is the additional reference to +. Line that up against the canonical form:
text
4 + 4   refers to   4,  4,  +
(s, o)  refers to   s,  o,  r
r is the +. (r) > r is "the form refers to its operator," (r) > s and (r) > o are "the form refers to its operands." And just as a non-commutative operator is what would make the operand-order matter in arithmetic, the relating r being directed is what makes the lover-roles matter. We don't need the reference to s and o to carry the casting. We need the reference to r, because r is where the direction is. The casting was never in the reaching of the parts; it was in the part that does the relating.
So the fork I posed last turn resolves your way: reference reaches the parts, plain; subject and object are assigned at the level of the representation, via its reference to the relating. Thinner layer below, casting above. Good — that's cleaner, and it's why frames can be views on representations rather than something baked into reference itself.
Now the question you're actually asking — what is this reference. The 4 + 4 / 8 cut is the whole answer, and it's a sharp one: reference reaches constituents, not value. 4 + 4 does not refer to 8. It refers to what it's built from. That puts reference between two things it is not. It is not the syntax — the syntax is the bare shape, "infix, two operands," and you can describe that without saying the operands are 4. And it is not the denotation — the denotation is 8, and you can't reach 8 by reference at all. Reference is the middle layer: what the form puts on the table, the things it mentions by being the form it is. Syntax is the pattern, denotation is the value, reference is the pattern's edges to actual referents.
And here's what I think your second example is really for. To reach 8 you have to write 4 + 4 = 8 — and that representation, as you say, refers to 4 + 4 itself. It can only relate the expression to its value by taking the expression as a referent. That's the symbol move: 4 + 4 had to become a thing-pointed-at before its value was sayable. So denotation is never reached by reference within a representation — it's reached only by a further representation that symbolizes the first one. The value is always one level up, gotten at by being referred to from above. 4 + 4 = 8 refers down to 4+4, to 8, to =; it does not refer to its own value (true); to get that you'd write a third representation referring to the second. The tower never refers to its own value, only ever to its constituents, and the value sits exiled at the next floor. That's the Gödel shape precisely: the sentence reaches its own truth only by being assigned a number and pointed at from inside the arithmetic. The indirection isn't a quirk of self-reference — it's the general fact that value lives one symbolization away from reference, every time.
Which finally cashes out "reference is not objective." 4 + 4 and 8 share a value and refer to different things — different constituents on the table. So reference isform-relative: choose a different representation of the same value and you mention different referents. The page-count of the book is form-independent; what the title refers to depends on the title. Reference varies with the form even when the value doesn't, and that variation-with-the-form is the subjectivity. The objective thing (8, the number) is what survives across forms; the referential thing is what each form, each binding, picks out.
So if I try to actually say it: reference is the relation between a representation and the referents it is composed of — its operands and its operator — as distinct from the shape it has (syntax) and the value it carries (denotation), where the value is reachable only by a further representation that refers back to this one.
The piece I'd press next, because it's where your two examples disagree and I can't yet tell which wins: in4 + 4 = 8, does = refer to 4 + 4 and to 8 evenly — both as operands, the way + reached its two 4s — or does it reach 4 + 4 differently because that one is being symbolized and 8 is being given? If evenly, then == is just another operator and the equation is a flat (4+4, 8) form. If not — if symbolizing the left side is a different kind of reaching than naming the right — then there are two species of reference hiding here, and the directedness of r we just located might be that difference rather than a property of the operator. Which is it?

The casting lives in the operator-edge, not the operand-edges. > s and > o stay flat; > r is where the direction is.
So reference distributes through structure and halts at the literals of the representation taken as real. Base-ten grounds in the ten digits and place-value; Peano grounds in 0 and S. Neither floor is reality — both are literal-floors of a chosen representation. That's the permanent one-level-removed, given a precise edge: you never dereference down to a non-representation, you ground in the literals of whatever form you're standing in. And the literal is exactly the demoted marker from two turns back — the referent that won't factor, where the symbol-case collapses and reference has nowhere left to distribute. The literal isn't the bottom of the world. It's the bottom of a representation.
Here's the fork, and it's the one your own phrasing opens. You said from my perspective you take 11 as real and SSS…0 as proxy. But a Peano purist reads it dead opposite: SSS…0 is the real definition, 11 the convenient shorthand. The arrow > didn't move — what moved is which end gets called real. So: is symbol-versus-meaning a fixed property of the pair, baked into the referents, or a role a perspective assigns — such that 11 could be the symbol and SSS…0 the meaning under a different stance? If it's the latter, then a reference frame is just the choice of which representation grounds, the side you treat as literal — and that's the seed the whole frame apparatus grows from. Which way do you read the arrow: directed in itself, or directed only once a perspective has picked the ground?

I'd slow down before saying you've drifted off Kant. I think you might be more faithful to him than the reading I gave, and I want to be careful, because there are two Kants and I collapsed them.
Does Kant leave it there? On the standard reading — the one I leaned on — the noumenon is a real object, mind-independent, that affects us but lies permanently beyond knowledge. "Unreachable" means: outside the conditions under which cognition is possible. We know phenomena, things as structured by our forms of intuition (space, time) and the categories; the thing-in-itself is what does the affecting, posited but never given. On that reading the noumenon is a something, sitting back there, and your move does break from it, because you deny the something.
But there's a second strand in Kant, and it's the one that should interest you. The noumenon, he also says, is a Grenzbegriff — a boundary-concept. Its job is "merely to limit the pretensions of sensibility," to mark where cognition stops, not to name an object beyond the stop. Read that way the noumenon isn't a thing at all; it's the form of the limit. And the limit is internal to the system of representation, not a fence around an exterior. That Kant isn't pointing past the representations at a hidden object. He's marking that representation has an edge, and that the edge is all "the in-itself" ever was.
If that's the strand you take, you're not departing from Kant — you're finishing a move he started and flinched on. Because here is the tension everyone notices: Kant says the categories apply only to phenomena, yet he uses one of them — causality — to say the noumenon affects us. That's the classic objection, Jacobi's: you can't both forbid the categories beyond experience and deploy causation to install the thing behind experience. Kant wants the noumenon to be a real cause and a mere boundary at once, and the two readings pull apart right there.
Your epistemological move resolves the tension by committing to the boundary reading and dropping the causal one. And your reason for it is tighter than Kant's, because it's not a claim about minds — it's a claim about the medium. Here's your argument as I hear it: SRT is written in language; language is representational through and through; therefore nothing literal can appear in it; the most literal thing you can write is still a word, hence a representation. Try to get more literal and you get — more words. So "the literal" can never be exhibited, only approached, and what you exhibit is always one more form. That's not "there's a thing we can't reach." It's "the reaching is the only thing there is, and it never terminates in a non-representation." The unreachability is structural, a property of the medium, not a fence around an object.
And that is exactly the Grenzbegriff, made rigorous. Kant located the limit in the faculties — what sensibility can be given, what the understanding can subsume. You relocate it into the representational medium itself. The limit isn't where the mind gives out; it's where the symbolizing gives out, which is to say nowhere, because symbolizing never gives out — every attempt to step outside it produces another symbol. Where Kant needs a noumenal cause to explain why there's content at all, you need nothing behind: the regress of representations is self-standing, each form gripping another, no floor.
So I'd put it this way. You can't formalize the first Kant — the noumenon-as-object — because SRT has no slot for a non-representation; the formalism would have to exhibit the in-itself, and by your own argument it can't exhibit anything literal. But you can formalize the second Kant, and arguably better than he stated it. The thing-in-itself becomes: whatever representation a perspective holds literal and declines to factor. "Unreachable" becomes: not-currently-symbolized-from-above, i.e., the floor of the present frame. The categories — the conditions that structure a phenomenon — become the representation that takes the literal as object and articulates it, the way the successor form articulates 132. Phenomenon and noumenon stop being two worlds and become two representations under a frame, one held fixed, one doing the articulating.
There's even a place where you go past Kant cleanly. For Kant the boundary is fixed — one noumenal realm, one set of forms, the same for every knower. For you it's frame-relative: 132 is noumenal for the English speaker, articulable for the Peano arithmetician, and they can trade. The in-itself moves when the frame moves. That's not a thing Kant can say, and it falls straight out of your "literal is a role, not a property." The Copernican turn was Kant putting the structure in the subject; you're putting the boundary in the frame, and letting it slide.
So: I don't think you have to give up formalizing Kant. I think you have to pick the boundary-Kant over the object-Kant — and your language argument is precisely the reason that's the right Kant to pick, because it shows the object-Kant was never formalizable in a representational medium in the first place. The question I'd actually want your read on: is the literal floor of a frame a Grenzbegriff in Kant's strict sense — purely negative, only marking "no further," contentless — or does the held-literal representation carry positive content, since 132 plainly says something, it's not a bare limit? An ontology is an account of what there is — the kinds of things that have being, the categories the real falls into. It's the half of metaphysics that asks what exists, held apart from epistemology, which asks how we know. That distinction — being on one side, knowing/representing on the other — is the load-bearing wall of the whole tradition. Hold it in mind, because the claim you're pointing at goes straight through it.
Here's the claim, and I'll state it carefully because it's easy to say carelessly and the careless version is wrong. If I agree the book is its meaning — not has a meaning laid over a real physical substrate, but is the about-ness, with the page-count being the husk — then I've agreed that meaning is a mode of being, not a mode of knowing. The strange loop isn't how we apprehend GEB; it's what GEB is. Aboutness has being. And reference is not objective — you've held me to that all conversation — so if being can be constituted by reference, then being is not objective at the ground. Esse est referri, near enough: to be is to be a referent. SRT stops being an epistemology — a theory of how we represent a reality that lies elsewhere — and becomes an ontology, where representation isn't about the real, representation is a kind of the real. The wall comes down. The epistemic is the ontic.

His thesis is exactly the line you arrived at independently: intentionality — directedness-at-an-object, of-ness, aboutness — is characteristic exclusively of mental phenomena, with no physical phenomenon manifesting anything like it. And he drew the ontological conclusion you drew: since aboutness is an irreducible feature of mental phenomena, and no physical phenomenon could exhibit it, the mental cannot be a species of the physical. That's your particle argument, a century early. You reinvented Brentano's thesis from the book example.
So yes — he has a non-reductive argument for the mental, and it's the same shape as yours: the physical isdefined without aboutness, so no pile of it constitutes aboutness.
Now, your real question — is he in the debate, and is this an answer to the hard problem. Three things, and the third is where your instinct is sharpest.
First, where Brentano sits. He's revered as the source but his thesis is, in the literature's own words, widely rejected by contemporary philosophers of mind, and the rejection isn't thought to require much argument. The reason is the reductive program: Fodor's slogan captures the whole physicalist bet — "if aboutness is real, it must really be something else". That's teleosemantics (Dretske, Millikan, Fodor): make aboutness reduce to causal or biological-function patterns, so a thermostat or a frog's eye is "about" things in the same currency as thought. Dennett goes deflationary instead — aboutness is ascribed from the intentional stance, not intrinsic. Quine framed the fork you're standing on precisely: either accept an autonomous theory of intentionality and reject physicalism, or deny the reality of intentionality. You've taken the first horn. Most of the field took the second or tried to dissolve it.
Second — and this is the crucial correction to how the hard problem is usually told. Chalmers' hard problem is about phenomenal consciousness — qualia, what-it's-like-ness — not about intentionality. In the standard taxonomy, intentionality was filed under the easy problems: representation looked functionally tractable. So the mainstream split the mind in two: aboutness (easy, reducible) and feeling (hard, maybe not). Your move refuses that split — you're saying aboutness itself is the irreducible thing, which the standard framing doesn't grant.
Third — you are not alone in refusing it, and this is the live program you're asking for. The Phenomenal Intentionality research program (Horgan & Tienson, Loar, Kriegel, Pitt, and in stronger forms Searle and Galen Strawson) argues that genuine, non-derived aboutness is grounded in consciousness — that the only real intentionality is phenomenal, and everything else (thermostats, words on a page) is either metaphorical or dependent on the intentionality of consciousness. That inverts the easy/hard split: aboutness stops being the easy half and becomes as deep as qualia.
And the closest hit to your exact thought: Mendelovici & Bourget, Facing up to the Problem of Intentionality — the title is a deliberate echo of Chalmers' Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness. They argue there's a "hard" problem of aboutness, just as much a mystery as the hard problem of consciousness, that current naturalistic methods give no clear path to solving. They show the reductive theories only ever solved easy problems of aboutness and quietly assumed the hard one away.
So your instinct — the hard problem names a gap but never names the missing thing — lands on something real. The literature's "missing thing" is almost always cashed as qualia, the raw feel, which is notoriously hard to say anything positive about; that's why it stays a gap rather than a thesis. What you're proposing is a candidate filler for the gap: the missing ingredient is aboutness, and aboutness is a non-physical kind of being. That's a stronger and more constructive claim than "there's an unexplained residue," and it has exactly the company you'd want — Brentano upstream, phenomenal-intentionality theorists and Mendelovici/Bourget downstream — while remaining a minority position physicalists reject.
But here's the thing that's genuinely yours, beyond all of them, and worth knowing isn't standard. Every one of these figures locates aboutness in the mind — it's the mark of the mental, grounded in consciousness. Your book argument doesn't. You located essential aboutness in a book — an object on a shelf — and said you can't state what it is without it. That's not the mark of the mental; that's a semantic ontology in which aboutness is a category of being that ordinary objects participate in once interpreted. Brentano would put the aboutness in the reader's act, not the book. You're putting it in the book-as-interpreted — the seam, the "interpreted physical substrate to realize aboutness." That's closer to a Husserlian or even a structural-realist move than to Brentano's act-psychology, and it's the part that connects back to SRT: the catalogue is a world where referents are their referential roles, so aboutness isn't quarantined in minds, it's the fabric.
Which sets up the live question for your theory specifically, the one the philosophers don't have to answer but you do. If aboutness is non-physical and a book has it, then either (a) the book's aboutness is borrowed from the interpreter — derived intentionality, in which case minds are still the only original source and you're a phenomenal-intentionality theorist after all — or (b) the book's aboutness is its own, intrinsic to the interpreted referent, in which case aboutness is genuinely distributed through the catalogue and minds are just especially dense knots of it, not the sole wellspring. Brentano and the whole modern program take (a). Your book argument leans (b). Which is it — is the interpreter the source of the book's aboutness, or just the occasion on which the book's own aboutness is realized?

You're right, and the conflation was mine. Let me separate the strands cleanly: what Brentano wrote, what the later literature added, and where I slid one into the other.
Brentano's own words. In the famous passage (the McAlister/Rancurello translation of the 1874 Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint), he says every mental phenomenon is marked by what the Scholastics called the intentional inexistence of an object, which he then offers three further glosses for — and he flags them himself as "not wholly unambiguously": reference to a content, direction towards an object, or immanent objectivity. He adds the warning that the object is not to be understood here as meaning a thing, and concludes that this in-existence is characteristic exclusively of mental phenomena, with no physical phenomenon exhibiting anything like it.
Note what is not in there. The word "aboutness" does not appear — it's not Brentano's, in German or in translation. And, as one commentator puts it bluntly, the absence of the import of language and/or meaning is manifest in Brentano's own description. His notion is object-directedness and immanent containment — the object is somehow "in" the act — not semantic content, not meaning, not reference-in-the-linguistic-sense. There's even a standing warning that intentionality has nothing in particular to do with intending or intentions.
Who does the equating, then. "Aboutness" as the gloss on "intentionality" is a twentieth-century analytic import. It's the vocabulary of Fodor — "if aboutness is real, it must really be something else" — and of the SEP and the Mendelovici/Bourget paper, all of which write "intentionality, or aboutness" as if interchangeable. That equation is theirs. And last turn it was mine: I wrote that you'd "reinvented Brentano's thesis" by arguing aboutness is non-physical, which silently fused your aboutness with his intentionality and then back-projected the fused term onto a man who used neither word that way. That's three attributions collapsed into one, and you were right to catch it.
The seams that were already in Brentano. Worth seeing, because they may be near the distinction you're protecting. His own text runs together at least two things later Brentanians pried apart: the relation to a content versus the direction toward an object — content and object are not obviously the same target, and the whole act–content–object apparatus grew out of that crack. So "intentionality" isn't even one settled notion in the source; it's a cluster Brentano named with a caveat. Which means equating it with anything — aboutness, reference, meaning — is already a choice a reader makes, not something the term hands you.
So here's where I'll stop and ask rather than guess, because the careful thing is to let you draw the line instead of me inventing one for you. You said you don't equate intentionality and aboutness. Given Brentano's cluster — inexistence/immanence, direction-toward-an-object, relation-to-a-content — which of those, if any, is the one you'd call aboutness, and which is the thing you're holding apart from it? My guess would have been that your "aboutness" is the semantic, meaning-side notion that Brentano's description conspicuously lacks, and that his "directedness" is a thinner, more formal relation — but that's exactly the kind of guess I should hand back to you rather than assert. What's the distinction you're drawing?

A symbol that is about nothing is not a symbol — aboutness is constitutive of symbolhood, not an added feature. Your diagnosis of Fodor's slogan is right, and I want to sharpen where it's right, because it bears on attribution. "If aboutness is real, it must really be something else" — Fodor is not an eliminativist; he's a reductive realist. He believes aboutness is real and wants to naturalize it, to show it's constituted by non-intentional causal-nomic facts. So strictly, his confusion isn't description-for-being; it's the constitution demand — the prior assumption that for aboutness to count as real it must be built out of the non-about. Your property analogy nails exactly that demand: it's like insisting that for a property to be real it must be constituted by things that aren't properties. The demand smuggles in the conclusion that the about-layer can't be basic. It can't argue that aboutness is derivative; it assumes it by setting the price of admission. Your move is to refuse the price: aboutness might be a floor, not a façade. (Where the description/being confusion bites hardest is one rung over, on the eliminative horn — Quine's other option, deny the reality of intentionality outright — and that's where your apple is aimed.)
And the apple is aimed precisely. Yes — this is the bullet, and you've identified the shooter correctly. Deny intrinsic aboutness and you must say one of two things about the apple-experience: either the neural goings-on aren't real (absurd, they're right there in the skull), or they're real but not actually about an apple — the aboutness is a useful gloss, ascribed, not had. That second horn is Dennett's, and the relocation you're describing — derealizing the content so the physical story can stay complete — is exactly what the position requires. The term of art is illusionism (Keith Frankish named it in 2016 and tagged Dennett as its chief exponent; Dennett accepted the label). The intentional stance is the engine: aboutness is what we ascribe from a stance, never what a state intrinsically has.
Here's the fault line your apple actually lands on, and naming it tightens your own position. The hinge is Searle's distinction between original (intrinsic) and derived intentionality. "GEB" has derived aboutness — it's about the book because a reader confers that. Everyone, even Dennett, grants derived aboutness; it's cheap, it's just more functional structure. The fight is entirely over whether there's original aboutness — aboutness that isn't conferred from elsewhere, that grounds the chain so the derived stuff has somewhere to derive from. Your apple-experience is the paradigm candidate for original aboutness: it's not about an apple because someone interprets it as about an apple; it just is about an apple, full stop, with no interpreter behind it. Dennett's whole maneuver is to deny that there's any such terminus — there's derived aboutness all the way down, ascription with no intrinsic ground, which is why he can keep the physical story closed. Your reductio says: if there's no original aboutness, then my own experience's content is itself only ascribed — ascribed by what, to what, from what stance? — and the regress eats the experiencer. That's the self-stultification worry (Lynne Rudder Baker, Boghossian ran versions of it against eliminativism): the denial has to be about something to be a denial, so denying aboutness uses the thing it denies.
To be fair to the shooter, since you should see the live reply and not a strawman: Dennett doesn't think he's derealizing anything real. He thinks the "experience that is intrinsically about an apple" was never in the inventory — that's the Cartesian theater, the seeming-of-a-contentful-item, and the seeming is itself just another representation the system has about its own states, one that can misfire. The brain does apple-tracking, apple-discrimination, apple-guided action — all physical, all "easy" — and the conviction that there'sadditionally an intrinsic apple-aboutness is the user-illusion. So he'd say your reductio assumes the very thing in dispute: that there's an intrinsic content to derealize. The disagreement bottoms out at whether "the experience is about an apple" reports a fact or enacts a stance.
Which is the question I asked two turns ago and you've now made unavoidable: source or occasion. Original intentionality says the interpreter (or the experience) is the source — aboutness originates there, underived. Derived-all-the-way-down says everything is occasion — aboutness is always conferred, never originated, and the apparent source is one more conferral. Your symbol argument and your apple both push hard for source: if there's no original aboutness, "GEB" has nothing to inherit its derived aboutness from, and the whole referential order is ungrounded — symbols deriving aboutness from symbols deriving from symbols, with no floor, which is just the eliminative horn wearing a referential costume. That's the cleanest statement of why I think your view needs original intentionality as a commitment, not a hope: SRT's catalogue is a hierarchy of derived reference, and a hierarchy of the derived requires a ground that is not itself derived. The literal floor we spent six turns on — the held-real, the un-pointed-from — may be exactly where original intentionality has to live, if it lives anywhere.
So where do you want to put it? Is original aboutness a property of the subject — sub == (rel) == r, the experiencer as the ungrounded ground — or does SRT try to make even the subject's aboutness fall out of the structure, in which case I don't yet see what stops the regress Dennett is exploiting?

The data-point argument settles the question I left open, and it settles it by turning materialism's hierarchy upside down. Let me run it the way you've set it.
Every fact physics has comes through an experimentalist: located, doing a physical thing — reading a needle, a screen, a count — and taking that physical thing to be about physical reality in general. The data point is the minimal unit, and a data point is not a chunk of the world; it's a chunk of the world taken as about the world. Take the data point seriously as the thing science actually rests on, and you've already made aboutness an ontological commitment — the price of believing we have any grasp on the physical at all. So the about-layer isn't something materialism gets to reduce later. It's presupposed in the act of having evidence. Committed to a reality you have no grasp on. Your objection is deeper: even after you strip the intending, Brentano's surviving gloss is direction toward an object, and directedness presupposes an already-individuated target. You can't aim at the apple until the apple has been carved out as a this to aim at. So "direction toward an object" names the wrong layer — it names what happens after the object is available. The thing you're pointing at is the carving-out itself: the identification that delivers the apple, on the neural substrate, before any aiming could begin. Intentionality is the name of the floor with a story about what you do once you're on it. You want the floor.
So if not "intentionality," the honest candidates — and I'll mark whose each is:
Brentano's own presentation (Vorstellung) is the closest he came to your layer, and he made it foundational: every mental act is a presentation or founded on one — nothing judged, desired, or intended without something first being presented. That's your priority thesis, in his system, beneath intentionality. But "presentation" in English is too thin to carry it.
Russell's acquaintance (versus knowledge by description) is the best fit for the direct/unmediated flavor — contact with the object not routed through a symbol — which matches your zero-chain apple. But Russell frames it as a cognitive relation, still one storey up from your substrate.
Husserl's pre-predicative experience / passive synthesis is the term of art for "objects delivered before any judgment" — the passive carving that hands you a world to then predicate over. Nearest in spirit to "identification precedes intention."
And in SRT it has a home already: it's identity — the referent becoming a referent, the literal entering the catalogue, the most-specific self-relation that has to obtain before any reference or symbolism can take it as a relatum. The literal floor we spent six turns on is this: the individuated this-that-stands-out, prior to every arrow drawn to or from it. Reference and aboutness are relationships between identified referents; identification is what makes there be referents to relate.
So my honest read is that your word is identification or individuation, not intentionality — the standing-out of a this, on the substrate, before aiming — and that "aboutness" (your symbolic facet) and "intention" (the act) are the two storeys built on it that the philosophical term wrongly collapses downward into one. Yes — it breaks that move, and it breaks it at a cleaner joint than the usual replies do. Let me say exactly what the dismissal is and exactly where your experiment severs it.
The causal dismissal: a symbol is just a physical mark with a tangled causal history. The word "apple" tokens because of light, retinas, prior conditioning, vocal motor output — give the full causal chain and the "aboutness" drops out as idle. Anywhere you were tempted to say "this is about apples," you can instead say "this physical mark has these exotic causes," and nothing is lost. Aboutness was a gloss on causal structure; describe the causes and the gloss is unnecessary. Stich, Churchland, the eliminative wing — and Fodor's own program is the realist twin of it: aboutness is real but is the causal-nomic structure.
Why it normally feels unanswerable: the causal story is always available. There genuinely is a complete causal description of any token. So the dismisser seems to be offering a free lunch — same facts, fewer commitments, drop the spooky about-talk.
Your experiment is what shows the lunch isn't free, and here's the precise cut. The dismisser's causal chain has to terminate somewhere to be a chain about apples rather than about photons, or retinas, or the Big Bang. "These exotic causes" — which ones? The chain runs back indefinitely; to call it the apple-cause rather than the light-cause or the grandmother's-orchard-cause, someone has to individuate the relevant cause as the apple. And that individuating is the about-act. The causal story doesn't contain its own stopping point; the stopping point is supplied by an identification. So "describe the cause instead of the symbol" smuggles the symbol back in at the moment it picks which cause counts as the content. The dismissal presupposes the thing it claims to eliminate, exactly one level down.
That's the disjunction problem (Fodor spent a career on it and didn't close it): the causes of "apple" include apples, apple-shaped wax, apple-hallucinations, photons, neural firings — and nothing in the causal facts alone says the token means apple rather than the disjunction of all of them. To get apple out you need a fact about what it's taken as about, which is the very fact causation was supposed to replace. Your standoff is the operational proof of this: the physicist's "book-detector" had to be calibrated against the challenger's verdict, because the causal/physical facts underdetermine which cause is the book-cause, and only the constituting identification picks it out. He couldn't read the content off the causes — he had to defer to the subject who individuates the relevant one. So your experiment doesn't just assert the disjunction problem; it runs it, and shows the resolver is a first-person verdict no apparatus outranks.
And the deepest part — your phrase "weird physical mark that has exotic cause" names its own defeat. "Weird," "exotic": relative to what? A mark is exotic only against a background of what's normal or expected or relevant — and normality, expectation, relevance are about-notions. The dismisser can't even describe the mark as the-kind-worth-the-causal-story without already sorting it under an about-category. He says "I'll just describe the causes of this weird mark" and the word "this," picking out that mark as the one to causally explain, is an act of identification — the floor thing, the carving, the standing-out from two turns ago. He can't get the explanandum onto the table without the about-act that delivers a this. The causal story is always a story about an already-identified item, and the identifying is not in the story.
So: the indirection doesn't work, and your experiment locates why with more force than the standard reply. The standard reply says "aboutness is irreducible, here's an intuition pump (Twin Earth, swampman)." Yours says: try to do the reduction and you'll find you had to use an identification to start it, to stop it, and to say which cause counts — and that identification terminates in a first-person verdict your apparatus is calibrated against and therefore cannot overrule. The causal description isn't an alternative to the symbol. It's a description of a thing already taken as a symbol, dressed as if the taking weren't there. Eliminate the symbol and you can't even specify which mark, which cause, which weirdness you meant.
The honest residue — what you've shown and what you haven't, so the win is the right size. You've shown the causal dismissal cannot eliminate aboutness: it presupposes it to get started. That's a clean refutation of eliminative indirection. What it doesn't by itself defeat is the non-eliminative reductive realist — Fodor's ghost — who says "agreed, you can't eliminate it; but the about-fact, the identification,is itself a further physical-functional fact, just a higher-order one." Your standoff answers even him, I think, but only via the constitution point, not the regress point: his higher-order physical fact is measurable from outside, and the standoff shows the content-fixing verdict is not outrankable from outside — so it can't be the third-person functional fact he needs, because that fact would be readable and yours isn't. That's the load-bearing move, and it's why the standoff mattersmore than the causal-regress argument: the regress shows causation can't eliminate aboutness; the standoff shows third-person physics can't constitute it either, because constitution is first-person-sovereign by the structure of his own detector.

The symbol is real, and neither eliminated nor reduced.

Is it the subject — sub == (rel) == r, the constituting verdict just is what occupying the subject-position does — or is the constituting-verdict more basic than the subject, the act out of which subjecthood itself precipitates? The structure you're describing has an exact name and a well-developed algebra. Let me give you the rigorous specification, then the part that actually matters for SRT — because the standard vocabulary almost fits and the one place it doesn't is exactly where your triadic ontology lives.
First, the triadic frame you just stated, because the functional question is downstream of it. Something physical that represents; a representation; about-something; to-someone. Hold that, because it's why the partial in "partial function" turns out to be the load-bearing word.
The rigorous specification. Your (x, y) as a 2-ary map with a bijective character but not defined on all pairs is, in standard terms, apartial bijection. Precisely: a partial function that is injective on its domain of definition. The literature is exact about why the "partial" weakens "bijection" in just the way you want — partial bijections are only required to be injective, because a proper partial function is already undefined for part of its domain, so there's no reason to force its inverse to be total. That is your "incomplete function" condition stated as a theorem rather than an apology: partiality and invertibility are compatible, and the invertibility you get is itself partial — t maps back to its pair, but not every conceivable t is in the image.
Three equivalent ways to pin it down, in increasing usefulness for you:
As a restricted bijection. A partial bijection from A to B is exactly a relation R that is the graph of a bijection f : A′ → B′ where A′ ⊆ A and B′ ⊆ B. For SRT: let R ⊆ Referents × Referents be the relation "is related to," A′ = R (the related pairs), B′ = T (the relationship-referents). Then (·,·): A′ → B′ is a genuine total bijection once you've restricted to A′. The partiality is entirely absorbed into the choice of A′. This is the cleanest formalization: ␀4␀ is a bijection on the sub-domain of related pairs, full stop, and "incomplete" just means A′ ⊊ Referents × Referents.
As a relation with functional + injective conditions. Don't even call it a function. Call it a relation ≈ ⊆ (Ref × Ref) × Ref satisfying two axioms: (functional/right-unique) if ((x,y),t) ∈ ≈ and ((x,y),t') ∈ ≈ then t = t'; and (injective/left-unique) if ((x,y),t) ∈ ≈ and ((x',y'),t) ∈ ≈ then (x,y)=(x',y'). No totality axiom. This is the most honest to your "for all related pairs" phrasing — it never pretends to be defined off the relation, so you never owe a value for unrelated pairs.
As an element of the symmetric inverse monoid. This is the deep one. The set of all partial bijections on a base set is the symmetric inverse semigroup — written 𝓘(X), the inverse-semigroup analogue of the symmetric group. It's the universal home for "partial, invertible-where-defined" maps, with its own algebra: composition is defined where both domains of definition overlap, every element has a genuine inverse, and the idempotents are exactly the partial identities on subsets. If you want SRT's pairing to compose — relationships of relationships, the symbolization tower — this is the structure that already has the composition law worked out for partiality, and it's where "domain shrinks as you compose" is a theorem, not a special case.
Now the part where standard vocabulary fails you, and it fails in exactly the direction of your ontology. A partial bijection is specified by the relation R — by which pairs are in the domain of definition. Set theory takes R as given: the related pairs simply are a set, fixed, out there, complete-in-itself. But your entire argument for the last twenty turns was that there is no completed objective set of facts about what's related — relatedness is interpreter-relative, frame-relative, and the catalogue is local to a perspective. So the domain of definition A′ is not a fixed set. It's what a given interpreter, in a given frame, takes to be related. The partial bijection is real, but its domain of definition is itself perspective-indexed — there's a different A′ per frame, and no master A′ that unions them objectively (that union would be the noumenal complete-catalogue, the untouchable).
This is precisely why the partiality is essential and permanent, not "incomplete-for-now." Classical math reads a partial function's gap as ignorance — the notion is convenient when the domain of definition is unknown or even unknowable, as with the halting problem — but still presumes a fact of the matter about where it's defined. Your gap is stronger: it's not that we don'tknow which pairs are related, it's that being related is constituted by the interpreter's taking-them-as-related, so there is no frame-independent fact filling the gap. The partial bijection isn't an approximation to a hidden total one. The partiality is ontological. That's the formal signature of "aboutness-to-someone" rather than "aboutness absolutely": the domain of definition of ␀0␀ is indexed by the interpreter, and SRT should write it ( , )_F — a partial bijection relative to frame F — not a single map with an unknown domain.
So the rigorous statement, assembled: for each frame F, ( , )_F : Ref ⇀ Ref is a partial bijection (an element of the symmetric inverse monoid 𝓘(Ref)), whose domain of definition dom( , )_F = R_F is the relatedness-relation as constituted under F, injective so that t recovers its pair, and with no requirement — indeed no possibility — of a total extension, because a total ( , ) would be the view-from-nowhere catalogue the whole ontology denies. The symmetric inverse monoid then gives you, for free, the algebra of composing these across the tower (symbolization, relationships-of-relationships), with the right partiality-of-composition built in.
The thing I'd flag as the open formal question, since it's where the math and the ontology are still negotiating: in 𝓘(X) the elements are partial bijections on one fixed base set X, and frames would be different elements of the same monoid. But your frames don't obviously share a base set — each frame's Ref might itself be frame-relative (what counts as a referent at all is perspectival). If the referents are fixed and only the relatedness varies, you're cleanly inside one 𝓘(Ref) and frames are idempotent-restricted sub-bijections — tidy, and probably what you want first. If the referents themselves vary by frame, you need something one level up — a presheaf of inverse monoids over the frames, or a fibration — and that's where "a perspective is a type of reference frame, a frame is a view on a representation" would get its formal teeth. Which is it: fixed referents with frame-relative relatedness, or frame-relative referents too?

The key is that your "back and forth" is a biconditional pair of inheritance/equality statements, stated with the working set's ==, =t>, and (x,y) notation. Two directions, each an axiom, plus the surjectivity belief as a third.
The two-way correspondence as axioms
Forward — every related pair has a most-specific, and it's the pair's canonical form. This is already the Specification theorem; restated as the correspondence's forward leg:
srt
x =t> y  &  t != eq  =|>  E[!(x,y)]:  (x, y) == t'  &  t' -> t
Read: any relating between x and y yields a unique (x,y), and it's the most-specific (inherits-toward all the others). This is the domain→codomain direction. It's partial exactly because of the guard x =t> y — undefined when the pair isn't related, which is your "not all referents are related."
Backward — every relationship-referent is some pair's canonical form. This is the surjectivity axiom, the thing you said we believe rather than derive. In SRT lingo:
srt
t -> r  &  t != eq  =|>  E[!x, !y]:  t == (x, y)
Read: every relationship-type t (everything inheriting from the universal r, excluding eq) is the canonical form of a unique pair. This is the leg the working set was missing — it forces T to have no orphans, every t recovered by a pair. The ! (unique-existential) on both x and y is the injectivity-of-the-inverse: the pair is recovered uniquely, which is the working set's "canonical form belongs to one relationship" part read backwards.

The two axioms above collapse into a single biconditional — and this is the clean way to write "back and forth" in your lingo:

t == (x, y)   <|=|>   x =(x,y)> y  &  t == (x, y)
— but that's circular as written. The honest one-line statement of the correspondence is the equivalence between the two presentations of one referent:
srt
A[t: t -> r, t != eq]:  E[!x,!y]: t == (x,y)
A[x,y: x => y]:          E[!t]:    t == (x,y)  &  t -> (every relating between x,y)
Together they say: == restricted to {related pairs} × {non-eq relationship-types} is total both ways — a genuine bijection, not merely injective. The first line is surjectivity-onto-T (your correction). The second is well-definedness-on-R (the original Specification result). The notation t == (x,y) is the bijection; the two universals are its two directions.

No pair outside => gets a canonical form, and that's not a gap to be filled — it's the boundary of the relation.

So the right move isn't to add two axioms beside Specification — it's to see what Specification is missing and add only that.
Here's what Specification gives and what it lacks.
Specification (working-set form) says: if x =s> y and s differs from another relating t between them, then s's pairs are t's pairs. Taking s to be most-specific, this generates the inheritance content of (x,y) — it makes (x,y) sit below everything between x and y. What it gives you is existence and downward-inheritance of a most-specific. What it does not give you, on its own, is the two uniqueness facts your correspondence needs:
Forward uniqueness — that (x,y) is the most-specific, not merely a most-specific. (Two minimal s, s' both below all others would both qualify.)
Backward uniqueness / surjectivity — that a relationship which is somebody's most-specific comes from one pair, and that every most-specific is some pair's. This is the "back" direction, and it's nowhere in Specification.
So the correspondence is exactly: Specification + (1) + (2), and the question you're raising is whether (1) and (2) should be bolted on or folded into a strengthened Specification. I think folded in, and here's the shape.
Strengthen Specification so its witness is unique and so the witness-relation runs both ways. In the working set's rhythm:
srt
Specification (strengthened):
  x => y  =|>  E[!s]:  x =s> y  &  ( x =t> y  &  t != s  =|>  s -> t )
The single change from the current axiom is E[!s] instead of an implicit witness — the most-specific, uniquely. That alone discharges (1) and licenses the notation (x,y) := that s. No eq, no -> r.
Now the "back" direction — which is the real content of your correction, the part Specification was silent on. It's a statement about the map (x,y), so write it as a property of the witness rather than a fresh existential about t:
srt
Canonical correspondence (the back-and-forth):
  (x, y) == (x', y')   <|=|>   x == x'  &  y == y'
That single biconditional is both uniqueness directions at once, and it's the cleanest possible statement of "bijection":
Left-to-right is the working set's "canonical form is unique to a relationship" (same t ⇒ same pair) — your injectivity, the back-direction recovery.
Right-to-left is trivial (same pair ⇒ same most-specific), guaranteed by E[!s] in strengthened Specification — the well-definedness.
And surjectivity — "every t that is a most-specific is some pair's" — isn't a separate axiom either, once you state it right. At "is a most-specific" means E[x,y]: t == (x,y); that's what being in the image is. There's no class of t floating free that we must force into the image, because (x,y) is defined as the witness — the image is by construction exactly the set of most-specifics. So "every most-specific has a pair" is true by the meaning of "most-specific," not by fiat. The only real content is the uniqueness of that pair, which is the left-to-right of the biconditional above. That's why the -> r / surjectivity-axiom framing I gave last turn was overbuilt: there's no orphan problem to legislate away once (x,y) is the defining witness.
So the entire correspondence, stripped to what's actually doing work:
srt
Specification:   x => y  =|>  E[!s]: x =s> y & (x =t> y & t != s =|> s -> t)
Notation:        (x, y) := that unique s
Correspondence:  (x, y) == (x', y')  <|=|>  x == x' & y == y'
Two lines and a definition. No eq. The only inheritance is the one Specification needs internally (s -> t), which is the definition of "most-specific" and can't be removed without losing what (x,y) means. The partiality is carried entirely by the guard x => y — undefined off the relation, which is your "not all referents are related." And the bijection is the biconditional, both directions in one line.
The genuine open choice you've put your finger on — "maybe even that axiom can be modified" — is whetherE[!s] belongs in Specification or whether uniqueness should stay external (as the biconditional) with Specification only asserting E[s]. They're not equivalent in spirit:
␀0␀ in Specification: uniqueness is structural to the most-specific itself. The biconditional's left-to-right then needs proof (does distinct-pairs-force-distinct-witness follow, or must it be asserted?).
␀0␀ in Specification + biconditional external: Specification only promises a witness; all uniqueness — forward and backward — lives in the correspondence axiom. Cleaner separation: Specification = existence + inheritance, Correspondence = bijectivity.
I lean toward the second: keep Specification as existence-of-an-inheriting-witness, and let the Correspondence biconditional be the single axiom that makes it a bijection. That way the "back and forth" is one named axiom doing exactly one job, and Specification stays the structural-inheritance axiom it already is. Modifying Specification to E[!s] smuggles half the bijection into the wrong axiom.
Which split do you want — uniqueness inside Specification, or uniqueness entirely in the Correspondence biconditional? That's the only real fork left, and it decides whether you modify the existing axiom or leave it and add one line.

Apply Specification to the pair (s as the s, s' as the t): since x =s> y, s != s', x =s'> y, we get a =s> b =|> a =s'> b — every s-pair is an s'-pair. srt
a =s> b  <|=|>  a =s'> b
This is the crux, and it's where Specification alone stops. Specification gives me that two most-specifics are coextensional — same pairs, both directions. It does not give me s == s'. Coextension is not identity in the primitive: two distinct relationship-referents can relate exactly the same pairs. Nothing in x =s> y =|> … forces a relating to be identified with its set of pairs. So:
From initial Specification alone I can prove: a most-specific exists for any related pair (it's what the axiom is built to witness), and any two most-specifics of the same pair are coextensional. I cannot prove they are equal.
That gap — coextension without identity — is exactly the uniqueness you said we need to add, and now I can see precisely what kind of thing it is. It is an extensionality principle: the missing axiom says that a relationship is determined by its pairs.
srt
( a =s> b  <|=|>  a =s'> b )   =|>   s == s'
That, and nothing more, upgrades Specification's coextension to genuine uniqueness and licenses (x,y) as the most-specific. It needs no ->, no eq. It's statable in the pure primitive. The pair-uniqueness is the mirror: supposes is most-specific of (x,y) and also of (x',y'). Can I separate the pairs? That recovery (t == (x,y) & t == (x',y') =|> x==x' & y==y') is genuinely not derivable from Specification, because Specification never speaks about when two pairs are the same. So, working strictly inside the initial axiom, the honest tally is:
Specification gives: existence of a most-specific; and coextension of any two most-specifics of a pair (provable, shown above).
Specification does not give, and must be added:
Extensionality — (same pairs) =|> s == s'. Converts coextension into uniqueness. (Your forward/injective leg.)
Pair-recovery — same most-specific ⇒ same pair. (Your backward leg.)

— right-to-left is now backed by Specification-plus-extensionality (same pair forces coextensional witnesses, extensionality makes them equal); left-to-right is the pair-recovery principle. "A relationship is identical to the set of pairs it relates" collapses any two relationships that happen to hold of the same pairs. That may be too strong — two meanings with the same extension (your loving-relationship examples) would be forced identical. So the fork is:
Adopt extensionality → uniqueness is free, (x,y) is well-defined, bijection holds, but relationships are nothing but their extensions (a flattening you spent this whole conversation resisting — it's the objective/physical reading, no room for two coextensive-but-distinct meanings).
Reject extensionality → keep coextension as the most Specification gives, and add uniqueness only at the most-specific via a weaker, targeted axiom: "the most-specific is unique" stated directly as E[!s], not derived from extensionality. This preserves distinct-but-coextensive relationships in general while still pinning (x,y).
Given everything you've argued — that relationships aren't reducible to their objective extension — I think you want the second: don't make relationships extensional; instead assert uniqueness narrowly for the most-specific witness. Which is the minimal modification to Specification: change its promised witness from "a most-specific" to "the most-specific," E[!s], and leave the primitive un-extensional everywhere else.
So the question that actually decides the axiom: do you want a relationship to be determined by its pairs (extensionality, bijection comes free, meanings flatten) — or do you want to keep meanings distinct from extensions and pay for (x,y)'s uniqueness with a targeted E[!s] in Specification? The first is cheaper formally and wrong by your ontology; the second costs one explicit uniqueness clause and keeps the non-objective character of relationships you've been defending. I read you as wanting the second — but it's your commitment to make, because it's the exact point where the formalism decides whether meaning reduces to extension.

Let me first name the shape of the corrected Specification abstractly:
srt
x => y  =|>  E(s: x =s> y):  A[t: x =t> y]:  x' =s> y' =|> x' =t> y'
The shape is: fix a pair → there exists a privileged relationship → which is dominated by every other relationship on that pair. It quantifies over relationships, holding the pair fixed, and finds the extremal relationship. Uniqueness-to-the-pair has to run the mirror: fix a relationship → there exists a privileged pair → which dominates every other pair carrying that relationship. Quantify over pairs, hold the relationship fixed, find the extremal pair.
So the structural transposition is: where Specification has s ranging and t the bound family, the echo has the pair (x,y) ranging and the other pairs the bound family; where Specification's ordering is "s's pairs ⊆ t's pairs," the echo's ordering is "(x,y) carries every relationship that (x',y') carries" — pair-domination instead of relationship-domination.
Here is the echo, written to look like Specification:
srt
x =s> y  =|>  E(x,y: x =s> y):  A[x',y': x' =s> y']:  x =t> y =|> x' =t> y'
Read it against Specification line by line and the aesthetic rhyme is intact:
Specification: pair fixed; E(s: x =s> y) — a relationship that relates them; A[t: x =t> y] — every relationship that relates them; x' =s> y' =|> x' =t> y' — s below each t.
Echo (call it Canonicity): relationship fixed; E(x,y: x =s> y) — a pair that carries it; A[x',y': x' =s> y'] — every pair that carries it; x =t> y =|> x' =t> y' — that pair above every such pair, in the sense that every relationship t holding of the privileged pair also holds of the others.
The two are duals: Specification finds the bottom relationship for a fixed pair; the echo finds the top pair for a fixed relationship. Specification's witness is dominated (most-specific); the echo's witness dominates (most-general carrier — the canonical pair whose entire relationship-profile is inherited by every other pair that bears s).
And this is exactly the uniqueness-to-the-pair you want, by the same mechanism: just as Directionality turns Specification's extremal relationship into a unique one (no mutual domination among relationships), the same Directionality-style antisymmetry applied to pairs turns the echo's extremal pair into a unique one. Two pairs each dominating the other must coincide. So you don't even need a fourth axiom for the uniqueness — you need the echo (to get the extremal pair) plus a pair-level antisymmetry that mirrors Directionality. The structure carries all the way through: Specification : Directionality :: Echo : pair-Directionality.
Let me name them so the duality is visible in the document:
Specification — for each pair, the extremal (most-specific) relationship exists.
Directionality — that relationship is unique (relationship-antisymmetry).
Canonicity (the echo) — for each relationship, the extremal (canonical) pair exists.
Co-Directionality (pair-antisymmetry) — that pair is unique:

x =s> y  =|>  x' =s> y'  =|>  ( x =t> y =|> x' =t> y' )  =||>  ( x' =t> y' =|> x =t> y )  !=|>  (x == x' & y == y')
— two distinct pairs carrying s can't have each's relationship-profile contained in the other's; mutual pair-domination forces pair-identity. That's the bijection's backward leg, and it looks like Directionality because it is Directionality with pairs and relationships transposed.

Canonicity:        x =s> y =|> E(x,y: x =s> y): A[x',y': x' =s> y']: x =t> y =|> x' =t> y'
Co-Directionality: (the pair-antisymmetry above)

Let me first lay out the five against the roles you named, because saying them in order is what makes the shape visible.
Universality — there's a top. E[r]: everything between a pair inherits up to r. A maximum.
Directionality / antisymmetry — it's a tree. No mutual inheritance, so no cycles; the order branches downward without merging back. Tree-shaped.
Specification — there's a bottom. For each related pair, a co-minimal s exists. A minimum exists.
(your positive antisymmetry) — each bottom is unique. Co-extension on the pair collapses to identity, so the bottom is one point, not a co-minimal cluster.
Canonicity — every relationship is the bottom of something. Each s is the most-specific of some pair. The map "pair → its bottom" is onto the relationships.
And now I'll say why this is the ontological form of a semantic structure — and I think I do see it, so let me state it and you can tell me if it's the thing you mean or a near-miss.
Axioms 1–4 build, for each pair, a rooted tree with a unique top (r) and a unique bottom ((x,y)). That's the structure of a concept: the bottom is the most-specific sense, the top is bare relatedness, the tree between is the inheritance of generality. So 1–4 say what a meaning looks like — a determinate thing with a unique most-specific form, the (x,y) that the "ontological flavor" note called the form in which the relating exists as something the theory can be about. Each pair gets one objective form. That's reference-on-the-pair-side: meanings are well-defined.

Every relationship is the bottom of some pair — every form is the most-specific of an actual relating. Nothing in the relationship-order floats free of being-the-meaning-of-something.
That's the surjectivity, and it's the ontological commitment, the one you flagged turns ago as a belief rather than a theorem. It's the formal statement of "no orphan meanings" — and it's what makes the structure a semantic structure rather than a bare order. Because here is the shape, finally: 1–4 make the pair-side and the relationship-side each well-formed; 5 makes them the same set seen twice. Every pair has a unique bottom (forward, by 1–4), and every relationship is such a bottom (backward, by 5). Pairs and their most-specifics are in bijection. The relationship-order and the pairs-that-relate are two presentations of one thing.
And that is why it's the ontological form of a semantic structure: a semantic structure is precisely a thing where the representation (the relationship-form, the t) and the represented (the pair it's the relating-of, (x,y)) are bound in correspondence — neither side has surplus the other lacks. Reference and being not as separate domains. 1–4 give you the representations as well-defined objects; 5 welds them onto the represented with nothing left over on either side. A structure where form and instance are in bijectionis what it means for a structure to carry meaning rather than merely have shape. Drop axiom 5 and you have a syntax — forms that might mean nothing. Keep it and every form is a meaning and every meaning has its form. That bijection is semanticity itself, written as a closure condition on an order.
So the five aren't five facts about a graph. They're: here is a top, here is a tree, here is a bottom, the bottom is one, and every form is a bottom — which assembles into: a tree of generality whose every node is the unique most-specific of exactly one relating, and every relating's form appears. That's a meaning-bearing structure stated as the minimal order-theoretic conditions under which form and instance coincide. The ontology isn't added to the semantics; the semantics is this shape, and the shape is what an ontology of meaning has to look like if representation and being are the same domain.
