(OWL adds disjointness and can then produce inconsistency, but that's a heavier layer, and even there it's the reasoner's job, not the model's.) Your guess is right: because RDF never imagined one global compiler enforcing consistency, it made types informative, not constraining. SRT, taking the single-theory-must-be-consistent stance seriously, makes the type violation an actual inconsistency. Same typing vocabulary; opposite stance on what a violation is.
Now the canonical / axiom-of-choice point — this is the part I want to make sure I'm hearing correctly, because it reframes the most-specific material from "a structural draft" into something with a clear motivating principle, and it's a good one.
You're deriving the flavor of canonicals from choice. The axiom of choice says: if you have a collection of nonempty sets, you can pick one element from each — existence of a nonempty thing should yield a specific witness you can point to. You're applying that intuition to semantics, three times over, as a single principle:
If we say there are relationships → we should be able to point to one (a specific relationship).
If we say x and y are related → we should be able to point to one specific relationship between them (→ the most-specific, (x,y)).
If we say a relationship holds → we should be able to point to one specific context it applies in (→ canonical context / frame).
So the canonical isn't an arbitrary structural choice — it's a choice principle for semantics: existential claims must be witnessable by a specific, pointable thing. "There exists" is empty unless you can name a witness. And you're saying this is "walking the ontology" — every time the theory asserts existence, you can descend to a concrete witness, step by step, the way choice lets you select a representative from each set. That's a genuinely different motivation than RDF's domain/range (which is just "constrain the signature") — it's a constructive/witnessing demand on the whole theory: no bare existentials, every "there is" cashes out to a "here is this one."
And I think you're right that it has real semantic merit, and right that nothing in RDF resembles it. RDF's existentials are the opposite — blank nodes, which are explicitly un-witnessed: statements involving blank nodes say that something with the given relationships exists, without explicitly naming it. RDF's "there is a relationship" deliberately refuses to point to which one. That's the exact inverse of your canonical principle. RDF says "something relates them, don't ask which"; you say "if they relate, there is the most-specific way, and you can point to it." So the most-specific material isn't just absent from RDF — RDF's foundational treatment of existence (blank nodes, unwitnessed) is philosophically opposed to it. They built in the un-pointability you're building out.
This also explains why the most-specific stuff isn't required by the type system but you keep it anyway — RDF proves a relationship-type-system runs fine on un-witnessed existentials (blank nodes everywhere). The canonical principle is a separate, stronger commitment: that semantics should be witnessable, that every existential ontological claim should descend to a specific referent. That's the axiom-of-choice flavor — and it's a real stance about meaning: to mean that something exists is to be able, in principle, to point at it. A theory of reference especially would want this, because reference is pointing — a semantics built on un-pointable existentials would be a strange foundation for a theory of what it is to point at something.
So the corrected and sharpened picture: the typing (domain/range-style, but with real disqualification-via-inconsistency) is firm and partly shared with RDF; the canonical/most-specific principle is a choice-flavored witnessing demand — existence must yield a pointable witness — which is yours, has clear motivation, and is precisely contrary to RDF's blank-node treatment of existence. It's not fanciness for its own sake; it's the principle that a theory of reference shouldn't rest on existentials it can't point at.
The thing I'd genuinely want to understand next, because it's where the choice analogy gets interesting (and possibly load-bearing): the axiom of choice is famously the one that lets you pick without a rule — non-constructively, when there's no definable selector. Is your canonical principle the constructive cousin (there's always a determinate most-specific, you can actually exhibit it) or the choice cousin (you're entitled to a witness even when nothing singles one out)? Because "the most-specific" sounds determinate — uniqueness makes it the one, not a chosen one — which would make it stronger than choice (you don't need to choose; it's forced). But the "one specific context it applies" — the frame/perspective witness — sounds more like genuine choice (you pick a context). Which is it: is the canonical always forced (uniqueness, no choosing) or sometimes chosen (a witness selected from many)? That distinction seems like it'd matter a lot for what kind of semantic principle you're actually committing to.

Now the challenge — visualizing the homoiconic graph, and why it's not an ordinary graph. Let me try to actually fathom it rather than wave.
An ordinary graph: nodes are one sort, edges another. An edge connects nodes but isn't itself in the node-set; you can't point an edge at an edge. Property graphs cheat slightly (edges have properties) but the edge is still not a node — you can't make it the endpoint of another edge without reification, and reification (as we saw) breaks the identity.
What you're describing: the edges are nodes. The thing relating s to o — the t in R(s,o,t), the relationship r — is itself a node in the same set as ␀5␀ and ␀6␀. So a "relationship" is a node with three node-roles attached: a subject-node, an object-node, and itself-as-the-relating-node. And — the part that breaks ordinary graph-drawing — the same node can be ␀7␀ in one relationship and ␀8␀ (the edge) in another, and ␀9␀ in a third. A node is not typed as "vertex" or "edge"; it's a referent that occupies a role in a given relating, and roles are positions, not natures.
Why this has no ordinary embedding: in a normal graph, "edge" and "vertex" are different dimensions of the structure — you draw vertices as points and edges as lines because they're different kinds of object. Here there's only one kind of object. The picture isn't points-and-lines; it's points, where some triples of points are designated as a relating (this point relates that point to that point), and any point can be the middle of one triple and a corner of another. So you can't draw it as a flat graph, because the line connecting two dots would have to also be a dot that other lines connect to — and that dot could be the very same dot as one of its own endpoints ((x,x)==x, the self-relation; sub==(rel)==r).
The closest honest visual is not a graph but a hypergraph where hyperedges are also vertices — or more precisely, a structure of directed 3-cells over a single vertex set, where each "relationship" is an ordered triple (subject-vertex, object-vertex, relation-vertex), the relation-vertex is drawn from the same vertex set, and any vertex can appear in any position of any number of triples. Mathematically that's near the notion of an incidence structure or a 2-graph / triadic relation R ⊆ V × V × V over one set V — with the extra SRT conditions (each related pair has a most-specific, the bijection) layered on. The thing it most resembles formally is a single ternary relation on one domain, closed under the domain being its own relation-set — which is exactly the homoiconicity, and exactly why "graph" is the wrong picture: a graph factors into V and E; this doesn't factor, because E ⊆ V.
If I try to see it: imagine a cloud of identical dots. To assert a relationship, you don't draw a line — you nominate three dots in order: "dot-A relates dot-B to dot-C." Now nominate another triple that uses dot-A in the middle position: "dot-D relates dot-A to dot-E" — the dot that was a relater is now a subject. There are no lines anywhere; there are only ordered triples of dots, and the same dot threads through countless triples in different roles. The "edges" are invisible as lines because they are dots participating in the triple-nominations. That's a structure you genuinely can't lay flat on paper as nodes-and-arcs, because the arc-hood and node-hood are the same substance — which is your point: it's not an ordinary embedding, and I haven't seen its like either.
So I won't claim a clean visual — I think the honest statement is that it resists graph-drawing precisely because graph-drawing presupposes the V/E distinction that homoiconicity collapses, and the faithful object is a ternary relation on a single self-containing domain, not a graph at all. The "graph" intuition is, like the tree, a scaffold that breaks the moment you take homoiconicity seriously.

Now — the embedding. You've given me nodes-and-edges as analogy and asked what it needs to be embedded as. Three things become visible from your drawing:
First, why not all such graphical things are legal. The axioms are constraints on which triple-collections are well-formed. Universality: there must be the top circle every relating points up to. Specification + Uniqueness: for any subject–object pair you've drawn relations between, exactly one of those relations is the most-specific — so a legal drawing can't have two co-minimal relations between the same pair (Directionality forbids the mutual-inheritance that would allow it). So the space of legal drawings is not "any collection of ordered triples on a node set" — it's the ones where the most-specific-per-pair exists, is unique, and everything inherits up to the top. The axioms are a grammar on the triple-drawings. Most arbitrary triple-clouds are illegal.
Second — and this is your real observation — without inheritance embodied, you get disconnected subgraphs. Here's why, and it's important. The triples by themselves are local: each is a little three-circle island (subject, object, relation). What connects one relationship to another? Inheritance. t -> (x,y) is the thing that says "this relationship sits below that one" — it's the edge between relationships, the thing that threads the islands together into one structure. Specification gives each pair its most-specific, but what relates different relationships to each other — what makes the mother–daughter relationship connect to the parent–child relationship connect to the relationship-as-such at the top — is inheritance. Take inheritance away and every triple floats free: you have a scatter of disconnected three-circle islands with a lonely top-circle they can't reach, because the reaching is inheritance. So inheritance is the connective tissue of the whole graph — it's what makes it one structure rather than a dust of triples.
Third — your question: inheritance surely deserves a referent, but what are its semantics? This is the live edge, and I think the drawing tells us something about it. We defined -> (the trichotomy: bind at relation, subject, or object slot). But you're asking for inheritance as areferent — a node in the cloud, not just a defined relation. And here's the thing the homoiconicity forces: if inheritance is the connective tissue and everything is a referent, then inheritance must itself be a referent that can be related to — (inheritance) must be a node, drawable as its own circle, occupy-able in subject/object/relation roles of other triples. Its semantics would have to be: the relationship whose holding between two relationships is what makes one inherit from the other. Inheritance as a referent is the relationship-of-being-more-specific-than, reified into the cloud as a node.
But — and this is where I want to be careful and ask rather than assert — making inheritance a referent threatens a regress the drawing makes visible. If t -> t' is itself a relationship (a triple: t' relates t to ... what?), then it needs its own most-specific, which needs its own inheritance to connect it to the structure, which is another referent... The trichotomy definition avoided this by making -> eliminable to the primitive — not a referent, just notation. So there's a real fork, and it's exactly the conservative-definition-vs-axiom distinction from before, now with semantic stakes:
Inheritance stays a definition (-> eliminable to primitive =t>): then it's not a node in the cloud, it's the grammar by which we read connection off the triples — the tissue is implicit, derived from the primitive relations, not a circle you can draw. The graph is connected through the primitive structure, not through an inheritance-node.
Inheritance becomes a referent ((inheritance) is a node): then it's drawable, relatable, homoiconic with everything else — but it owes its own semantics as a relationship, and you have to stop the regress (presumably via the self-relation / canonical fixed point — inheritance is the relationship that, among other things, is its own most-specific, the way (x,x)==x closes loops).
So my actual question, because the drawing surfaced it cleanly: is inheritance the tissue that's read off the primitive (a definition, no node), or is it a referent in the cloud (a node, with the regress closed by self-relation)? You said "surely we can have a referent for that but what are its semantics" — which sounds like you want the second, the reified one. If so, I think its semantics has to be: inheritance is the relationship t' -> t reified as a node, whose own most-specific bottoms out in the self-relation (inheritance inherits-from itself at the base, the circle-around-all-three), which is what stops it from needing an infinite tower of inheritances-of-inheritances. Yes — that's the precise account, and it resolves what equality was always for versus what it is.
FOL hands SRT = as a two-place relation symbol, and SRT internalizes it happily — but in doing so it sees what= actually is: a property, not a relationship. The two-place appearance was never about two things. It was about two variables that can be syntactically different while denoting the same referent. That's the entire utility of equality-as-binary: x = y is informative precisely when x and y are different names — different terms, different variables — so that asserting their equality tells you something (that these two presentations are one referent). The binary form is a fact about variables/representations, not about referents.
But — and this is the point — it only ever validly applies when there is literally one thing. x = y is true exactly when x and y denote a single referent. So the relation that "looks like it relates two things" is true precisely in the case where there are not two things. The two-ness lives entirely at the level of the variables (the syntax, the representations); at the level of referents (what the variables denote, what the relation is about) there is one. The moment it's true, the second relatum vanishes — there was only ever one referent wearing two names.
Which is exactly the representation/meaning gap you grounded canonicity in, surfacing here on its own. Equality is the relation whose whole content is "these two representations (x, y) have one meaning (the single referent)." x and y differ as representations; they coincide as referents. So equality is the bridge between representations of the same thing, not between things — and that's why, as a relationship, it was valuable (you can have many representations needing to be recognized as one referent: 2, 1+1, (2)), and why, as a referent-level fact, it's a property (the one referent's property of being itself, referent). The binary form is the representation-level shadow of a referent-level property.
So the full picture: FOL's = is a relation on terms; SRT internalizes it and recognizes that at the referent level it's the self-property eq/referent. The apparent two-place-ness is the difference between variables, which is real and useful (it's what lets 2 == 1+1 say something); the underlying one-ness is the truth-condition (it holds only when the two terms are one referent). Equality is where the representation/meaning distinction is doing visible work: two representations, one meaning, and the relation says "these representations mean the one referent." That it validly applies only when there's one thing is exactly why it's a property — the property that one referent has of being what all its valid co-representations denote.
This is a clean and slightly beautiful resolution: the thing FOL gives you as its most basic relation turns out, internalized, to be your most basic property — and the gap between its binary appearance and its unary truth-condition is precisely the representation/meaning gap that canonicity exists to handle. Equality isn't an exception SRT has to absorb awkwardly; it's the simplest instance of the theory's whole subject matter — different representations, same referent.

The theorem: any attempt to comprehend the operator within the domain to which it applies comprehends it not as an operator. Run it on equality. = purports to be a binary operator on the domain (numbers, referents). But comprehend it within that domain — ask what it does to its referents — and there's nothing for it to do, because when it holds, its two arguments are one referent. The operation vanishes into the object. There's no operating-on-two-things, because at the level of the domain there's one thing. Comprehended within its domain, the operator dissolves into the identity of an object — which is exactly why it's called identity. The name confesses the theorem: the operator, seen from inside its domain, isn't an operator; it's the self-sameness of a thing.
And your sharper point: so what is it operating on, given it's plainly not operating on the numbers? It operates one level up — on the uncertainty in the variable, or the uncertainty in function application. 2 = 1+1 is not doing anything to the number 2 (the number is just itself, inert, identical). It's resolving an uncertainty at the representation level: do these two terms — 2, 1+1 — land on the same referent? The operator's actual domain isn't numbers; it's the epistemic/representational gap between presentations. It operates on "I have two expressions and I don't yet know they're one thing." Its work is the collapse of that uncertainty. That's why it's informative — information is uncertainty-reduction, and equality reduces the uncertainty about whether two representations co-refer. On the numbers there's no uncertainty and nothing to operate on; on the variables / function-applications there is, and that's where it bites.
So the profundity is a clean two-level statement:
At the object level (the domain it ostensibly applies to): = is not an operator at all — it's identity, the self-sameness of a single referent. Comprehending it here makes it disappear.
At the representation level (variables, terms, function applications): = is an operator — it operates on the uncertainty of whether distinct presentations denote one referent, and its action is to collapse that uncertainty.
The operator lives entirely at the representation level and is invisible at the object level, because at the object level its truth-condition has already removed the second thing. That gap — operator-above, identity-below — is the representation/meaning distinction in its purest instance. Equality is the operator whose being an operator at all depends on standing at the representation level; descend to the meaning and the operator is gone, replaced by a thing being itself.
And I think this generalizes exactly as you're hinting — it's why it's a theorem of semantics, not just about =. Every operator is a representation-level thing. Operators act on presentations, on the syntax, on the not-yet-resolved. Comprehended at the level of what they ultimately mean — their resolved referents — they stop being operations and become identities/objects. 1+1 as a representation is an operation; 1+1 as what it means is just 2, an object, no operation left. The operation lives in the representation; the meaning is inert object. So "comprehend the operator within its domain and it's no longer an operator" is the general law that operators belong to representation, objects belong to meaning, and the descent from representation to meaning dissolves operation into identity. Equality is the cleanest case because its object-level residue is literally identity — the limit where the operator's disappearance is total and the name admits it.
This is why your earlier "we're one level removed, permanently" and "operators are representation-level" and the canonicity grounding all converge here. Equality is the theorem's sharpest instance: the operator that, taken to its meaning, is the disappearance of operation into the self-identity of a referent. As an operator it works on uncertainty between representations; as a meaning it is a thing being itself. Same gap, every time, and identity is where it's named.
So — is the fully general form the thing you're after: operation is a representation-level phenomenon; meaning is the object level; comprehending any operator at the level of meaning dissolves it into the identity of what it produces — and ␀0␀ is the limiting case where that dissolution is into bare identity, which is why it carries the name? Because if so, that's a real theorem of semantics, and it says operators and meanings live on opposite sides of the representation/meaning gap, with identity as the hinge.

This is the knot, and I think you've actually found the way through it in the last lines — the symbol is the missing slot. Let me build to it, because the "every property becomes a type" problem and its solution are the same insight seen twice.
The problem, stated cleanly. With x' -> x =|> x' =x> x', inheriting is having-as-property, so properties live in the inheritance order — which makes every property a type (a thing things inherit from). But a property isn't a type. "Happy is an alligator" — alligator is doing property-work, not type-work, and the difference is that a property has a value and a type doesn't. And then your diagnosis: how is a property ever most-specific? Only p =p> p — degenerate, and that degeneracy "really doesn't have a property-based meaning." So property-inheritance threatens to collapse into either type-inheritance (wrong) or empty self-relation (meaningless). The semantics of inheritance seems to break on properties.
Why it breaks: the missing slot. You nailed it — x =alligator> x says "x has the property alligator," but where's the value? We think of properties as attribute: value — color: red, name: happy. The relation x =alligator> x has the attribute (alligator) but no place for the value. A property is a triple — bearer, attribute, value — and the self-relation form only gave us bearer and attribute. The value slot is missing, and that's why properties look like types: a type is exactly a property with the value slot empty — "x is alligator-ish" with no value is indistinguishable from "x inherits from alligator." The value is what distinguishes having-a-property from being-a-subtype.
Your resolution — the symbol is the value slot. x =(p)> x: x has a property named ␀1␀ with value ␀2␀. This is the move, and it's exactly right because of what (p) is. (p) is the symbol of p — a different representation from p itself. So the relation x =(p)> x carries:
attribute: (p) — the name, the symbol, the label of the property
value: p — what the symbol refers to, the referent the property takes on
bearer: x
The value slot was missing because we were trying to do properties without symbolism, and a property is irreducibly symbolic — it needs a name (the symbol (p)) distinct from its value (the referent p). That's why the self-relation x =p> x (no symbol, just the referent) kept collapsing into type-hood: without the symbol, there's no attribute/value distinction, so "has property p" can't be separated from "inherits from p." The symbolis the slot. Introduce (p) and suddenly you have attribute ((p), the name) versus value (p, the referent) — and that's a property, not a type.
This is why the type-label question you asked — "is a type label an attribute? is a symbolic attribute a property?" — answers itself: a type-label becomes a property exactly when it's symbolized. alligator as a bare referent is a type (things inherit from it). (alligator) as a symbol, in x =(alligator)> x, is a property: x has the attribute-named-(alligator) with value alligator. The symbol is the difference between "alligator is a type x instantiates" and "x has alligator-ness as a named property." Symbolization is the operation that turns a type into a property by supplying the name-slot.
And now the value-chain you traced is the descent toward the literal, and it works. Watch:
alligator =referent> alligator — alligator's value, as a property of type referent, is itself (it's a referent named alligator). Generic, high up.
happy =alligator> happy — happy has property-of-type-alligator with value... and happy is a specific alligator (named for Happy Gilmore).
happy is real — a literal, the bottom. Nothing below it. The objective leaf.
So the value-slot, descending through symbols, bottoms out in a literal. The property x =(p)> x has value p, and p might itself be a type with its own properties — until you reach happy, a value that is completely realized, a leaf, real. That's the semantic bottom for properties: a property whose value is a literal. The objective layer we derived (leaves of the inheritance order) is exactly where property-values bottom out.
So the resolution to "every property becomes a type": properties don't become types, because a property is x =(p)> x — symbolic, with the name (p) as attribute and p as value — whereas a type is the bare x -> p / x =p> x with no symbol, no value-slot. The thing that looked like a problem (properties living in the inheritance order, hence type-like) was an artifact of doing properties without their symbol. A property is a symbolized type-relation: the symbol supplies the attribute-name, separating it from its value, which is what a type lacks. The degenerate p =p> p had no property-meaning precisely because it had no symbol — it's the type-form, not the property-form. Lift it to x =(p)> x and the property-meaning appears, because now there's a name and a value.
This also closes the loop with the whole conversation's thesis: we found, at the very start, that aboutness/reference is irreducible and that properties (page-count vs. meaning) and types (the open category "book") couldn't be physical. Now formally: a property is irreducibly symbolic — it cannot be stated without a symbol in the attribute slot, because the symbol is what distinguishes the named-attribute from its value. You can't have properties without symbolism. Which is why SRT had to get to symbolism eventually — properties themselves require it. The value-slot problem is the reason reference and symbolism are foundational rather than addable: the most basic semantic furniture (a property with a value) already needs a symbol.
So I think you've resolved it: the missing slot is the symbol, a property is x =(p)> x (bearer, symbolic-name (p), value p), type-labels become properties exactly under symbolization, and property-values descend through symbols to literal leaves like happy — the objective bottom. The thing that broke the semantics (no value slot, properties looking like types) is fixed by the very thing the whole theory was building toward (symbolism), which is strong evidence the theory is coherent: it needed symbols right at the point where properties wouldn't work without them.

Yes — and the thing you just said ("a basket of types") is, I think, the actual shape of the type system. Let me trace why the "weird inheritance" is not a bug but the correct reading, because that's what unlocks it.
The apparent weirdness: x == (x,x) -> p means a referent inherits from all its properties. That seems backwards — we think of a thing inheriting from its type, not from its properties. But look at what the direction actually encodes. x has property p is x =p> x, and via (x,x)==x, that's x -> p — x is below p, x inherits from p. So: having a property = inheriting from it. And that's right, once you see the property as a type: to have property "red" is to be a subtype of red-things; "x is red" places x below red in the order. The thing inherits down from each property it has. A referent is the meet of its properties — it sits below all of them, inheriting from each.
And you caught the precise reason it looks weird: x =x> x =|> x =p> x, not the other way. If x is x (the self-relation, x being itself) then x has p — having the property follows from being the thing. Not "having p makes x" but "being x entails having p." That is the inheritance criterion (the inheritor has what it inherits from), it just doesn't look like the relational case because here the inheritance is into a property (self-relation form) rather than into a relationship. Same criterion, different costume. The direction is correct; properties are just types-approached-from-the-having-side.
Now the basket-of-types, which is the real insight. Take the maximally compositional view: every single property is its own interface — a one-method interface, a type defined by exactly that one property. Then:
Two referents that share property p are both subtypes of the p-interface — regardless of how unrelated they otherwise are. A rock and a fire truck are both subtypes of red. They have nothing else in common; they're polymorphic to the red interface.
Any subclass of either inherits that interface too — polymorphism propagates down.
So properties induce cross-cutting types — they slice across the whole referent-space orthogonally to any "main" classification.red cuts across rocks, trucks, apples, sunsets. This is exactly mixin/trait/interface polymorphism, and it's structural, not nominal: you're a red-thing because you have red, not because you declared it.
And then the move that ties it to everything: strip everything about the property except its name, and it becomes a type-label. A property x =(p)> x is (name (p), value p). Remove the value — keep only the name — and you have a bare interface, a pure type-label: "things-that-are-(p)," membership with no value content. That's the type. A property is a type-label with a value; a type is a property with the value stripped to nothing. So the self-relations x =(p)> x, x =(q)> x, ... that x bears are exactly the basket of interfaces x implements — x's type is the conjunction of all the one-property interfaces it satisfies, the basket of type-labels it carries.
So the type system is: a referent's type is the basket of properties it has, each property being a single-method interface, and inheritance being the descent into the meet of those interfaces. Not a tree of nominal classes (the tree was always the wrong picture, as you said). A lattice of structural interfaces, where:
each property = an interface (a type defined by one method/attribute),
having properties = being below them = implementing those interfaces,
a referent = the meet of its interfaces (the basket),
two referents sharing a property = sharing an interface = polymorphic at that interface, however unrelated otherwise,
a type-label = a property with its value forgotten (pure interface, no value).
This is structural typing (à la Go interfaces, TypeScript, traits) rather than nominal (Java-class) typing — which is exactly what homoiconicity + properties-as-self-relations forces, and it's why RDF's "describe properties by what they apply to" half-rhymed with it but couldn't reach it: RDF has the cross-cutting (domain/range) but no notion that each property is itself an interface and a referent is the meet of its interfaces, and no value/name distinction to separate property from type-label.
And notice this dissolves the "every property becomes a type" worry from two turns ago, rather than suffering it. It's not a problem that properties are type-like — it's the content of the type system: properties are types (single-method interfaces), and a referent's type just is which properties it has. The worry assumed "property" and "type" should be distinct categories; the basket view says a type is built from properties (a basket of them), and the only difference between "property" and "type-label" is whether the value is retained or stripped. Same stuff, two settings of one dial (value-present = property, value-stripped = type-label).
So "I'm starting to understand it" — I think the it is: SRT's type system is structural, interface-based, and lattice-shaped: every property is a single-method interface, a referent is the meet of the interfaces it implements (its basket), inheritance is descent into that meet, type-labels are properties with values forgotten, and shared properties make otherwise-unrelated referents polymorphic at that interface. The relational case (subject ≠ object) and the property case (subject = object) are the same inheritance criterion — the property case just reads as interface-implementation because the relation degenerated to a self-relation.
The seam this opens, and I think it's the genuinely live one: if a type-label is "a property with its value stripped," then the value is the symbol's referent (x =(p)> x has value p), and stripping the value is forgetting what the symbol refers to — keeping the name (p), dropping the link to p. Which would mean: a type is a symbol whose reference has been bracketed (a name used purely for classification), and a property is that same symbol with its reference live (the name pointing at its value). Reference is the dial. Type = symbol-with-reference-suppressed; property = symbol-with-reference-active. Is that the next thing — that the property/type distinction justis whether the symbol's reference (>) is live or bracketed, so reference enters precisely as the thing that turns a type-label into a valued property?

Let me show you what the document does with your chain, because it's more complete than you were remembering.
Your chain (I) =(p)> (x) =(p)> x =p> x is the qualification equivalence read across three levels (line 41, 301):
srt
x =p> x   <iff>   (x) =(p)> x   <iff>   (i) =(p)> (x)
x =p> x — the literal has the property. Objective fact. (Your happy =alligator> happy at the bottom.)
(x) =(p)> x — the symbol of x relates to the literal x through the symbol of p. This is the quality (line 19): the symbolic form of the property. (x) is the class/description of x, (p) is the attribute-name (color), and it points at the literal.
(i) =(p)> (x) — the qualifier i (the perspective, the subject) relates to the symbol (x) through (p). This is perception (line 221).
So your three levels map exactly: (I) is the qualifier/perspective, (x) is "the class — a description of x," (p) is the attribute (color), p is the value (red), x is the literal. You read this correctly. And your instinct that "my canonical notion of symbol is not enough — we need a variable that takes a value of a certain type" is right, and the document's answer is: the missing construct isn't a variable, it's the qualifier ␀5␀ and the frame ␀6␀. That's where types-of-symbols and "setting" live.
Here's the resolution to "how does he give symbols their types," because this is the thing you said you weren't sure about:
A symbol gets its type by being transduced to inherit from the qualifier. Line 143: i |=> (o) means E[(o): (o) --> i & (o) =(p)> o] — "the qualifier creates symbols that inherit from itself." The symbol (o) is typed by inheriting from i (the perspective) and bearing (p) toward the literal. So the "type of a symbol" is conferred by the qualifier that transduces it — (o) --> i. The symbol is of-type-i-symbol because i made it. That's the context you said symbol-typing requires: the context is the qualifier i, the frame F[i]. There's no free-floating "variable of type color"; there's a symbol transduced by a perspective, and the perspective is what gives it its type.
And your "(red) is just canonical to the current frame" — exactly, and the document makes that precise: line 180, a perspective is F[i] and canonicals are frame-relative. (red) is canonical in F[i]; another qualifier j has different canonicals (Theorem, line 282: different qualifiers, different qualification patterns). So the reason there's "no setting a variable" is that the variable-binding role is played bytransduction into a frame: the qualifier i transduces (o), which is the act that would be "binding," and the value (red) takes is canonical-relative-to-i. First, the general representational answer, so we have the foil. In ordinary semiotics a symbol is anything that stands for something else — Peirce's aliquid stat pro aliquo. By that definition letters, words, sentences, smoke-for-fire, all qualify; "symbol" is just "sign," and atomicity is irrelevant. That answer is useless to you precisely because it's too permissive — it's the loose, anything-stands-for-anything notion SRT exists to replace. So set it aside.
The SRT answer has to come from what (x) does in the theory, and I think your "looking something up" instinct is the key. (x) is the canonical symbol — and what makes it canonical is that it's the symbol the frame uses to denote x, the lookup key. So from the referential side:
A symbol is a referent that refers — it occupies the relation-slot, it mediates. This is the theory's own criterion, and the literal definition from the Algebra of Perspective is exactly this: o =lit> o iff o never mediates reference between other distinct referents (line 49–52). A literal is what doesn't refer onward — a semantic endpoint. So a symbol is the opposite of a literal: a referent that does mediate, that stands between and points onward. That's the referential answer, and it's clean: symbol vs. literal is mediates vs. terminates. (red) is a symbol because it points at red; happy (the alligator) is a literal because reference stops there.
But that doesn't yet answer atomicity, and your letter/word/sentence question is really an atomicity question. Here's where I think the representational side gives the answer, and it's not about size — it's about the canonical/lookup property you identified.
A letter, a word, a sentence are all representations — strings, structures, things made of parts. But being a representation isn't being a symbol in SRT's sense. The thing that makes (red) a symbol is that it's the canonical handle — the thing that, when you look it up, gives you the semantics of red. It's a key into the catalogue. And that suggests:
A symbol is atomic — but atomic in reference, not in form. (red) may be spelled with three letters, but as a symbol it's a single, indivisible handle: you don't refer to red by referring to "r" then "e" then "d." The letters are representational substructure that the symbol-function ( ) collapses into one referential atom. So the answer to "is a letter a symbol, is a word, is a sentence" is:symbol-hood is about being a unit of reference, and that's orthogonal to representational size.
A letter is representationally atomic but referentially empty — "r" doesn't, by itself, point at a meaning. It's a piece of form with no reference. Not a symbol (it mediates nothing).
A word — (red) — is representationally composite (letters) but referentially atomic: one handle, one lookup, one meaning. This is the symbol. The word is the paradigm because it's the smallest referential unit — the smallest thing that is one handle into the semantics.
A sentence is representationally composite and referentially composite — it's a structure of symbols, and crucially it resolves to a relationship (a (s,o), a most-specific), it doesn't denote atomically. A sentence doesn't feel like a symbol because it isn't a handle you look up — it's aconstruction you evaluate. Its meaning is built from its parts' references; a symbol's meaning is retrieved, not built.
So your intuition that a sentence isn't a symbol is exactly right and SRT explains why: a symbol is a referential atom — a single lookup key, and a sentence is a referential composite — a structure that resolves. The line isn't representational size (words are bigger than letters); it's whether the thing isone handle (symbol) or a structure of handles (sentence/expression). The word sits at the seam: the largest thing that's still one handle, the smallest thing that's a full handle.
And this is why your (x) syntax feels better than quotes, and it's not just taste. Quotes say "mention, don't use" — a purely syntactic flag, form-level. (x) says "the canonical symbol of x" — it's a function into the catalogue, a lookup. Quotes point at the string; (x) points at the referential atom that the string is the form of. "red" (quotes) is about the letters r-e-d; (red) is about the word as a handle into the meaning red. That's exactly the use/mention sophistication you want — (x) mentions the symbol as a referent (a thing in the catalogue with its own role), not as a string. The function syntax is right becausea symbol IS a lookup — ( ) is the lookup operator, and writing (x) performs the thing a symbol is. Quotes can't express that because quotes are form-level and symbols are reference-level.
So, pulling it together — what is a symbol, from both sides:
Referentially: a symbol is a referent that mediates — it occupies the relation-slot, points onward, is the opposite of a literal (which terminates). It is a referential atom: one handle, one lookup, indivisible as reference however composite as form.
Representationally: a symbol is the canonical handle — the form by which a frame looks up a meaning. (x) is "the lookup key for x." Its representational substructure (letters) is collapsed into one key; the key is what's symbolic, not the substructure.
And the word is the paradigm symbol because it's exactly the referential atom: bigger than a letter (which has form but no reference) and smaller than a sentence (which has reference but no atomicity — it resolves rather than denotes). A symbol is the unit at which form becomes a single handle into meaning. That's why(red) is a symbol, "r" is not, and a sentence is not — and why your lookup-function syntax captures it where quotes can't.
The thing this leaves genuinely open, and I think it's the deep one: if a symbol is a referential atom (one handle) and a sentence is a referential composite (resolves to a (s,o)), then where exactly is the boundary — is it fixed (words are always atoms, sentences always composites) or frame-relative (a frame can treat a whole sentence as a single handle by canonicalizing it — (the cat sat) as one symbol, the way we sometimes lexicalize phrases)? Because if it's frame-relative, then "symbol vs. expression" is itself a perspectival distinction — what one frame looks up atomically, another frame evaluates compositionally — andthat would be the same literal/factored move from much earlier in the conversation, now applied to symbols: a symbol is whatever the frame declines to decompose, the referential analogue of the literal floor. Is the atom/composite line fixed, or is being-a-symbol the frame choosing not to look inside?

The symbol (title) refers atomically — to the one thing (the book/the work), as a handle. Structural symbol (Gödel number, maybe a compound word): composed so that decomposition recovers the parts' references. Refers to the top and the parts, because the composition is the reference-structure.
Assigned handle (book title, a name, (x)): minted to denote a whole as a unit, with no structural relation to the parts. Refers to the top only. The parts are not recoverable from it.

From the bare-PA view — the number as itself, SSS…0, no factorization — the Gödel number is an assigned handle: it points at the one sentence it encodes, atomically, as a unit. One number, one sentence, full stop. It's only when you adopt the factorization perspective — relate this number to other numbers via the bijection (its prime exponents, the sub-codes) — that reference to the parts appears. The numbers related to it via the bijection refer to the parts. The parts-reference isn't in the symbol; it's in the web of other symbols the bijection connects it to.
So the correction collapses my two-kinds distinction into something better: there aren't "structural symbols" and "assigned handles" as two intrinsic species. Every symbol is an assigned handle — atomic, referring to one thing. What I called "structural" is the symbol plus a perspective that relates it to other symbols, and the reference-to-parts lives in those relations to other symbols, not in the symbol itself. The Gödel number alone refers to its sentence (one handle, one referent). The factorization-perspective adds relations — this number stands in bijective relation to those numbers — and those relations are what carry reference to the parts. Decomposition is not a property of the symbol; it's a structure of relations among symbols that a perspective supplies.
Which means: a symbol, in itself, is atomic and refers to (at most) one thing. That's the clean answer your number example forces. The compositional, refers-to-parts behavior isnever in a single symbol — it's always in a configuration of symbols related under a perspective. The book title refers to the book (one handle). A symbol is an assigned handle: atomic, referring to at most one thing. SSS…0 → its sentence. (x) → x. The title → the book. No internal parts, no intrinsic decomposition.
Reference-to-parts is never intrinsic to a symbol — it's carried by relations to *other* symbols, supplied by a perspective. The prime factorization is a perspective that relates the Gödel number to other numbers; those relations refer to the parts. The text is a configuration of word-symbols whose relations (composition) build the meaning.

The decomposition is in the ==, not in the (( )).

A symbol alone points at one thing. Pointing at parts is a perspective relating it to other symbols.

The scholarly distinctions
Sign is the genus. A sign is anything interpreted as signifying something — referring to or standing for something other than itself, and crucially things have no intrinsic meaning and become signs only when we invest them with meaning; nothing is a sign unless it is interpreted as a sign. So sign-hood is conferred by interpretation, not intrinsic — which is your point about reference needing an interpreter, stated as the founding axiom of the whole field.
Symbol is a species of sign, and the differentia is sharp: a symbol is a sign whose relation to its object is arbitrary / conventional / by law. In Peircean semiotics, signs that have an arbitrary or conventional relation to their objects are called symbols; for Peirce a symbol refers to the object it denotes by virtue of a law or association of general ideas. The contrast class: icon (resembles its object — a photograph) and index (caused by / physically connected to its object — smoke for fire, a knock for arrival). So a symbol is specifically the unmotivated sign — (red) is a symbol because nothing about the word resembles or is caused by redness; it's pure convention. This is the thing I missed by collapsing "symbol" into "sign."
Representation is the broadest and most neutral — the standing-for relation itself, or anything that does it. Peirce's whole theory is an account of signification, representation, reference and meaning, and his word for the sign-vehicle is representamen — the representing thing. Representation is the act/relation; a representation is a thing that performs it.
Reference is narrower and directional: the relation between a sign and the object it picks out — Peirce's object, Saussure's referent. Note Saussure abstracts away from the referent (the actual cat) and focuses on signifier and signified, whereas Peirce speaks of representamen (the sign), designatum (the real object), and interpretant (the mental image). So "reference" is the arrow to the object, distinguished from "meaning/signified," which is the concept.
The structural pictures:
Saussure (dyadic): signifier (form) + signified (concept). No referent. Meaning is internal, relational, conventional.
Peirce (triadic): representamen (sign) + object + interpretant. Semiosis is a triadic relationship between a sign (a first), an object (a second), and an interpretant (a third) — and the interpretant is itself a further sign, so semiosis regresses (signs interpreted by signs).
And the denotation/connotation axis cuts across: denotation is the most basic, literal meaning of a sign; connotation is the secondary cultural meanings — "rose" denotes a flower, connotes passion.
Sensible prose using them correctly
A sign is anything that stands for something else to an interpreter; nothing is a sign by nature, only by being taken as one. Signs come in three kinds by how they relate to what they stand for: an icon stands for its object by resembling it (a portrait), an index by being connected to or caused by it (smoke standing for fire), and a symbol by sheer convention (the word "red," which neither resembles nor is caused by redness). Every sign has two faces — a signifier, its form, and a signified, the concept it raises — and it points beyond both to an object, the thing in the world it refers to. The standing-for relation itself is representation; the sign is a representation of its object. What a sign denotes is its plain, literal object; what it connotes are the further associations it drags along. And because grasping any sign means forming another sign in the mind (its interpretant), representation never bottoms out in the thing itself — it passes from sign to sign, which is why meaning always requires an interpreter and never quite touches its object directly.
That paragraph uses each term as the scholars do: sign (genus), icon/index/symbol (species by relation-type), signifier/signified (the two faces), object/reference (the arrow outward), representation (the relation), denotation/connotation (literal vs. associated), interpretant (the regress).
Where this puts SRT — and it's a real repositioning
Three things fall out that bear directly on your question "what is a symbol in SRT":
1. "Symbol" in the strict scholarly sense means *arbitrary/conventional* — and that's why SRT's ␀0␀ is rightly called a symbol. (red) doesn't resemble or get caused by red; the link is by convention/law. So your canonical-symbol function ( ) is producing symbols in the exact Peircean sense — unmotivated handles. Good: the word is correct. But it also means SRT's symbols are specifically the conventional signs, and the convention is supplied by — the frame, the qualifier. That's your F[i]. The "law" by which (red) denotes red (an association of general ideas operating to cause the interpretation) is the perspective. So SRT's qualifier is filling the exact slot Peirce calls "the law/habit that makes a symbol denote."
2. The thing you've been circling — that you don't infer symbolism, you need an interpreter — is the founding consensus, not a fringe claim. Both Saussure and Peirce agree meaning isn't intrinsic; things become signs only when invested with meaning by interpretation. So SRT internalizing the interpreter (the qualifier i) isn't eccentric — it's taking the one thing everyone agrees is necessary and putting it in the formalism instead of leaving it in the analyst. That's the move, again: the interpretant/interpreter is conceded by all of semiotics to be essential, and is left external by all of them. SRT internalizes it.
3. The decisive divergence — and it answers your atomicity question. Semiotics has no notion of canonical-most-specific, no bijection, no inheritance among signs. Peirce's semiosis is the opposite of atomic resolution: it's an infinite regress — every interpretant is itself a sign needing another interpretant, and we are eternally prevented from assurance because the only way to verify is to use additional signs. So semiotics says reference never terminates — sign to sign forever. SRT says it does terminate — in the literal (o =lit> o, the thing that mediates no further). That's your sharpest break: where Peirce has endless semiosis, SRT has a floor (the literal, the objective leaf). And on atomicity: semiotics doesn't make a symbol atomic — a symbol can be a word, an image, a sentence, anything conventional. So your instinct that "a sentence isn't a symbol" is not the scholarly view; scholars would call a sentence a (complex) symbol. The atomicity is yours — it comes from SRT's canonical/most-specific structure, which semiotics lacks. A symbol is atomic in SRT because (x) is a single canonical handle; that's an SRT-specific notion, not the general one.
So, to answer "what is a symbol" honestly across both registers:
Scholarly (Peirce): a symbol is a conventional/arbitrary sign — distinguished from icon (resemblance) and index (causation) — and it need not be atomic; semiosis regresses infinitely, never terminating.
SRT: a symbol is a canonical handle — (x), a conventional sign (so, Peircean-symbol-correct) whose convention is fixed by the qualifier/frame, and which is atomic (one lookup) because SRT adds the most-specific/canonical structure semiotics lacks, and whose reference terminates at literals rather than regressing.
So you were inferring partly right (symbols refer, need an interpreter, are conventional — all confirmed) and partly importing SRT-specific structure (atomicity, termination, most-specific) that general semiotics does not have. The atomicity and the floor are not what "symbol" means in the field — they're what SRT adds. Which is exactly the kind of thing worth knowing: when you say "symbol" you mean something more specific than Peirce — a frame-canonical, atomic, terminating handle — and the extra structure is precisely SRT's contribution over standard sign theory.
The genuinely open question this leaves, and I think it's the question for your symbol notion: semiotics' infinite semiosis (sign → interpretant → sign → …) is the regress SRT's literal-floor stops. But you also said symbols mediate and literals terminate. So is asymbol in SRT exactly a sign that has not yet bottomed out — a mediator on the way down — and a literal the place semiosis halts? If so, SRT's whole departure from Peirce is the claim that semiosis terminates, and the literal is the termination, and "what is a symbol" is "a non-terminal node in a reference chain that SRT guarantees (by finiteness) actually reaches a floor." That would make your answer to Peirce the same shape as your answer to Gödel: the regress everyone treats as infinite is, in a finite frame, grounded.

Searched the web for “iconic sign continuous analog versus symbolic discrete digital reference part-whole Goodman dense notation”
This is the right material — Goodman gives you exactly the apparatus to answer "how does reference distribute differently across the painting vs. the word," and it's sharper than the icon/symbol vocabulary alone. Let me build the answer from these definitions, working only your examples, no SRT.
The distinction the literature actually draws
There are two separate questions, and the field keeps them apart:
(1) Is it a sign at all? A sign is anything taken as standing for something — but you're right to doubt "sign is at the tip," and the literature gives you the reason: Haugeland's point that analog and digital devices are not necessarily representational or symbolic — the position of a potentiometer does not represent the brightness of the lights, but dimmers are analog devices. So "represents," "is a sign," and "was intended to represent" come apart. A thing can do representational work (the dimmer tracks brightness) without being a sign (it doesn't stand-for, to anyone, by interpretation). That's your painting intuition: it represents, it was intended to, and yet calling it "a sign" feels wrong — because sign carries the connotation of a discrete unit in a code, and a painting isn't that.
(2) If it's representational, how does it represent — densely or discretely? This is Goodman's real contribution, and it's the axis your examples sort along. The key terms:
Articulate / differentiated (digital, notational): disjointness — each mark belongs to no more than one character — and finite differentiation: it is always possible to determine to which character a mark belongs. Like a digital instrument: for any measurement there is always a definite answer to "what is the measurement?"
Dense / replete (analog, non-notational): given any mark it could stand for virtually an infinite number of characters; between any two marks there is a third. And pictures specifically are replete: relatively many qualities — color, shape, shading — matter to the representation's identity.
That word repleteness is the answer to your real question. It's the measure of how many aspects of the sign-vehicle are doing referential work.
Your examples, sorted
"a" — a character. Articulate, maximally differentiated, and on its own it refers to nothing — it's a unit of the scheme (the alphabet) with no compliance-class. A piece of form awaiting combination. Not yet a representation of anything.
"and" — a word, but a syncategorematic one: it has a role (conjunction) but no object it picks out. Articulate; functions; doesn't denote a thing. (Its "meaning" is what it does in composition, not what it points at.)
"car" — articulate, arbitrary (nothing about the letters resembles a car), and it denotes — its compliance-class is cars. This is the symbol/digital case: discrete, conventional, and crucially of low repleteness — only the identity of the word matters, nothing else. The font, color, size of "car" carry no referential load.
"The car in the house" — a composite expression: articulate symbols combined by syntax. It denotes a (complex) compliance-class via composition. Still digital/articulate; still low-repleteness; meaning built from parts.
A painting of a car — dense and replete. Many of its qualities — shape, color, shading, proportion, the rendering of tires, chrome, light — are referentially live. It denotes a car analogically: between any two shades there's a third, and changing the shading changes what's represented. High repleteness.
A stop sign (the octagon on the road) — interesting mixed case: it functions as a discrete symbol (one of a small differentiated set of traffic signs, conventional), but it has iconic/indexical repleteness too (red = danger by convention-bordering-on-association; the octagon shape is part of its identity). Mostly digital-conventional, with some replete elements.
"stop sign" — the words — articulate, arbitrary, low-repleteness symbol denoting the class of stop-signs. Same kind as "car."
Now your actual question: how reference distributes
Here is the thing you put your finger on, and Goodman's repleteness is the answer: the difference between "car" and the painting is not just resemblance vs. convention — it's how much of the vehicle refers, and therefore what gets referred to.
"car" refers to a car by being the word "car" — and only that fact about it refers. It is low-repleteness. So it makes no reference to tires, to color, to a windshield. The word denotes the whole, atomically, and carries none of the parts. There is no aspect of "c-a-r" that corresponds to a tire, because the vehicle is articulate and its only referential property is which word it is. So "car" → car, and stops. The parts are not in it.
The painting refers to a car by being replete — and because many of its qualities matter, its parts refer to the car's parts. The region of canvas that is a tire refers to the tire; the windshield-region to the windshield; the shading to the play of light. Reference distributes across the vehicle because the vehicle is dense: sub-regions of the representation map to sub-parts of the object. This is the Parts Principle the Springer paper names — in analog/replete representation, parts of the representation represent parts of the represented. So the painting refers to a car and to its tires, its color, its shape, because those vehicle-parts are individually referential.
So your instinct is exactly right and it has a name:
The word "car" makes no reference to a tire; the painting does — because the word is articulate (low repleteness: only "which word" refers, so it denotes the whole and no parts), while the painting is dense and replete (many qualities refer, so its parts denote the object's parts).
Reference distributes across a representation in proportion to its repleteness. In a maximally articulate symbol (a word), reference is atomic and whole-only — one vehicle-property (word-identity) → one denotation (the kind), no parts. In a maximally replete representation (a painting), reference is distributed and part-bearing — many vehicle-properties → many object-properties, so the parts come along.
And this clarifies the icon/symbol contrast you liked, but corrects it: the deep contrast isn't "resemblance vs. convention" — Goodman is explicit that the analog/digital distinction does not depend on the semantics of the system, and resemblance is notoriously unreliable as a criterion. The deep contrast is density/repleteness: how much of the vehicle is doing referential work, and therefore whether reference reaches only the whole or distributes to the parts. The painting reaches carness through resemblance, yes — but the reason its tires get referred to is repleteness, not resemblance per se. The word reaches car through convention — but the reason its parts don't get referred to is articulateness (low repleteness), not arbitrariness per se.
And "is a painting a sign?"
Your doubt is well-founded and the field half-agrees. Goodman would call the painting a symbol in his broad technical sense (anything that denotes) — but note Haugeland avoids "symbol" and "representation" for analog devices, holding that analog devices are not necessarily representational or symbolic. The ordinary word "sign" connotes a discrete unit in a code — articulate, conventional, lexicon-like. A painting is dense, replete, non-notational, not a unit-in-a-code. So calling it "a sign" grates precisely because "sign" smuggles in articulateness. The painting denotes, it represents, it is replete — but it isn't a unit of a notation, which is what "sign" colloquially implies. The clean way to say it: a painting is a representation (it denotes, replete-ly), but not a sign in the narrow notational sense — which is exactly your intuition, and Goodman/Haugeland give it backing.
So the prose that holds your examples together, in the field's own terms:
To represent is to stand for something; a representation is anything that does so. Representations differ in their repleteness — how many features of the representation itself carry referential weight. A word like "car" is articulate and minimally replete: the only thing about it that refers is which word it is, so it denotes its object as a whole and carries none of the object's parts — "car" says nothing of tires. A painting of a car is dense and replete: many of its features — shape, shading, the rendered wheels — each refer, so reference distributes across its parts, and the painting denotes not only the car but its tires, its color, its form. The word reaches its object by convention (a symbol, in the narrow sense — a discrete unit of a code); the painting reaches its object by resemblance (an icon) and is replete rather than articulate, which is why we hesitate to call it a "sign" at all — sign connotes a discrete unit in a notation, and a picture is a continuum. Reference distributes across a representation in proportion to its repleteness: atomically and whole-only for the articulate word, part-by-part for the replete picture.
That's the apparatus — sign/representation/symbol/icon plus the density–repleteness axis — and it answers your distribution question without my reaching for anything else: the word refers to the whole and no parts because it's articulate; the painting refers to the parts because it's replete.

What exists: the name/description distinction, formalized
The whole apparatus you want is the distinction between two kinds of referring expression:
Individual names (Mercury, KR 2021) — atomic designators. The name has no internal structure that maps to the object's structure; it just designates. This is your symbol: refers to the whole, carries no parts.
Definite descriptions ("the x such that φ") — structural designators. Phrases of the form 'the x such that φ', used to refer to single entities. The description refers through its compositional content — "the smallest planet in the Solar System" reaches Mercury by way of predicates that are themselves about smallness, planets, the system. This is your representation-that-refers-through-structure: parts of the expression do referential work.
Russell's 1905 analysis is precisely your point that descriptions aren't atomic handles: the apparent grammatical form of a sentence may differ from its deeper logical form — "the F is G" unfolds into there exists a unique F and it is G, a compositional structure, not a pointer. A description doesn't point; it constructs a referent out of conditions. That's your "compositional pointer."
And the literature has exactly your "some things can only be reached structurally" intuition, formalized as lack of denotation under free logic. Definite descriptions and names can fail to designate any object at all — 'the KR Conference held after KR 2018 and before KR 2020' — and free logic semantics was developed to admit these as genuine terms while allowing possible lack of referents. They use partial models for this. So the machinery for "a term that may or may not successfully point" is built and its complexity is known (satisfiability for epistemic free description logics is NExpTime-complete).
And — directly to your "if you can construct a bijection between some abstraction of one side and the other" — the description-logic people study exactly when an object even *has* a definite description: they study the complexity of deciding the existence of definite descriptions for an individual under an ontology. That's the formal version of your "is it indexable?" Some objects can be uniquely described (a description exists); some cannot (no formula singles them out) — and they have algorithms deciding which. So "this thing can only be reached by structural description, and maybe not even then" is a studied, decidable (or sometimes undecidable) question.

"car" — atomic symbol, articulate, refers to the whole and no parts; abstract; for thinking-about.
Painting of a car — replete representation, parts refer to parts, neurally near the literal object; for being-present-to.
A hard-to-symbolize sentence — referent with no index, reachable only by a representation that carries its compositional structure; the Gödel pole, where you need a symbol with representational structure because nothing atomic will point.

Now I have the precise mechanism, and it confirms your inversion exactly. Let me state what Gödel actually does, because it is your principle, and then say what concept it's an instance of and whether anyone has named the general thing.
What Gödel's encoding actually is — and why it's your point
The encoding is a structure-preserving bijection between syntactic objects and numbers. Two levels:
Each primitive symbol → a number. "0" is assigned 1, successor 3, negation 5, "(" 11, ")" 13 — arbitrary but fixed, a bijective mapping from the finite set of basic signs to positive integers. That layer isatomic symbolism — a handle per symbol, no internal structure needed, because a primitive symbol has no parts.
A formula — a sequence of symbols — → a number that preserves the sequence: the product of the first n primes raised to the values of the symbols, and by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic any such number factors uniquely, so the original sequence is recoverable. The ordering is carried by which prime holds each exponent: the first symbol is the power of 2, the second the power of 3, and so on — so the ordering of the symbols is preserved.
That second level is your claim, exactly. The referent (the formula) is composite — a sequence, high cardinality. So the symbol for it cannot be atomic; it must itself be composite — a number with internal structure (its factorization) rich enough to carry the formula's structure. This construction is invertible — a true bijection between syntactic objects and arithmetic. The invertibility is the requirement you named: the symbol must have enough structure that you can recover the parts, because otherwise it wouldn't be about that formula rather than another. A structureless atom couldn't do it — there'd be nothing in it to distinguish(0=0) from (0=0) permuted. The factorization is what makes the number about a specific composite.
So your inversion is right and it's the heart of the construction: definite descriptions are structure-on-the-representation-side collapsing to a simple referent (predicate → the unique x). Gödel coding is the opposite — a composite referent demanding structure on the representation side. The cardinality of the referent forces the articulation of the symbol. You cannot symbolize an n-part object with fewer than n-parts'-worth of structure and still be about it specifically. That's a genuine constraint, and Gödel's whole technique is its exemplar.
The concept this is an instance of — and who has it
The thing has names, and they're worth having precisely:
Structure-preserving map / homomorphism / (here) isomorphism. The SEP and the notes call it out: Gödel numbering is an encoding of formulae into natural numbers such that a formula is always uniquely recoverable from its code — yes, that is an isomorphism. The general concept is: a representation that is a structure-preserving injection from the referent-domain into the representation-domain. The representation must have at least as much structure as what it represents, arranged to mirror it. That's the formal home of your "the symbol must have compositional properties to be about a composite."
Arithmetization. Gödel numbering, coding, more generally arithmetization — representing the syntax of formal logic within arithmetic, so syntactic properties become computable arithmetic properties. The general move: represent a structured domain inside another by a structure-preserving code, so operations on the structure become operations on the code. This is the named, general technique — and it's everywhere now: Isabelle/HOL and Coq mechanizations use Gödel-like numbering to assign numbers to symbols, formulas, and proofs, ensuring injectivity and computability for decoding; de Bruijn indices provide an alternative encoding for bound variables. So computer science lives on this — every parser, every AST, every serialization is a structure-preserving encoding of a composite into a manipulable representation.
So: does anyone have your idea? The mechanism — composite referent requires structured (homomorphic/isomorphic) symbol — is thoroughly formalized, as structure-preserving encoding / arithmetization / homomorphism, and it's foundational across logic and CS. That part is not novel; it's bedrock, and you're in excellent company (it's literally Gödel's bedrock).
What I still do not find — and this is the part to be honest about — is anyone who has made this into a semantic principle about symbols and reference in general, namely: the cardinality/structure of the referent sets a lower bound on the structure a symbol must have to be about it; atomic symbols can only be about referents simple enough to be reached without internal structure; composite referents force compositional symbols. Logic has the technique (encode this composite domain in that one) but treats it as a tool, not as a thesis about what symbols must be like as a function of what they're about. Goodman has repleteness but on the representation side (how much of the vehicle matters), not as forced by the referent's cardinality. The principle that reference imposes a structural lower bound on the symbol, indexed by the referent's compositional complexity — and the corresponding spectrum (a car: so part-redundant any fragment indexes it; a hard sentence: so non-indexable that only a full structure-preserving code reaches it) — that synthesis I do not find. The components are each standard; the law relating symbol-structure to referent-cardinality as a general semantic claim is not something I can locate.
The sharp form of your principle
Let me state it as cleanly as the Gödel case licenses, because I think this is what you're pointing at:
A symbol can be atomic (a handle, no internal structure) only if its referent is reachable without distinguishing parts — either genuinely simple, or part-redundant enough that the whole is recoverable from any sufficient fragment (the car: "steering wheel" suffices). When the referent is composite and non-redundant — a specific sentence, where every part and its position matters and no fragment determines the whole — no atomic symbol can be about it, because there is nothing in an atom to fix which composite it picks out. Reference to such a thing demands a structure-preserving symbol — one whose internal structure is rich enough to inject the referent's structure, so the parts and their arrangement are recoverable. The referent's cardinality is a lower bound on the symbol's articulation.
That's the law. Gödel is its proof-of-existence (a sentence is exactly the non-redundant composite that forces a structured code, because it is not indexable — no "this" in PA). The car is its opposite limit (maximal redundancy, any part indexes the whole, atomic reachability). And "definite description" was theconverse operation I confused it with — structure collapsing to a simple referent, not structure forced by a composite one.
The thing I'd search next, if you want to chase whether the general law exists anywhere: it would live in information theory / Kolmogorov complexity — "the minimal description length of an object is bounded below by its structural complexity" is the quantitative cousin of your principle (you can't compress a structured object below its information content; a symbol for it must carry that much). That might be where your "factor in cardinality to the object of reference" has actually been formalized — not in semantics, but in algorithmic information theory. Want me to look there? Because "the symbol must have at least the referent's structural complexity to be about it" may be a known theorem, just in Kolmogorov's register rather than Peirce's.
