That makes sense as a dependency, and it's the right shape for one — the philosophical paper has to do the work that licenses SRT's ambition, because without it SRT is a formalism in search of a mandate. Let me say what I think the paper actually has to establish, since you're working on it and a clear target helps.
The zombie argument gets you to "materialism is false, consciousness is fundamental" — if you win the conceivability→possibility step. But for SRT specifically, you need more than the negative result (materialism false). You need the positive thing Chalmers left thin: a reason to believe the subjective and objective belong in one domain related by an internal relation, rather than two domains bridged by an external psychophysical law. Because that's the load-bearing commitment SRT makes that Chalmers doesn't — Chalmers' property dualism leaves you with two kinds of properties and ad-hoc bridging laws; SRT says they're one domain with the relation inside. So the paper has to motivate the single-domain-with-internal-relation claim, not just the materialism-is-false claim. Those are different, and the second is the one SRT needs.
I think there are a few load-bearing things the paper has to do, and it's worth being clear which is the hard one:
1. Win or sidestep conceivability→possibility. This is the contested step, the live battleground (type-B materialists grant conceivability, deny possibility). You have options here, and which you pick shapes everything: (a) defend the inference directly (Chalmers' two-dimensional route — hard, much-attacked); (b) grant the battleground is a stalemate and argue SRT doesn't need full possibility, only that the epistemic gap is real and ineliminable, which is enough to motivate a wider representational ontology even if the metaphysics stays contested; or (c) go Russellian-monist — which I'd flag as probably your most natural ally, see below. Which one you take determines whether the paper is making a strong metaphysical claim or a more defensible epistemic-cum-representational one.
2. Motivate single-domain over two-domain. This is the SRT-specific part and I don't think the zombie argument gives it to you for free. Property dualism is also compatible with the zombie. So is interactionist dualism. So is Russellian monism. The zombie under-determines which post-materialist ontology — it just rules out reductive physicalism. So the paper needs an additional argument for why the right post-materialist ontology is one domain where relationships (including the psychophysical one) are referents, rather than two-domains-plus-bridge. That argument can't come from the zombie; it has to come from something about reference itself or about why bridging-laws-as-external are unsatisfactory (the "thin/ad-hoc" critique of Chalmers' psychophysical laws is your opening — you can argue that an external bridge is explanatorily idle in exactly the way Chalmers' critics say, and that internalizing it is the only way to make the relation do work). That's the move I'd watch most carefully, because it's where the paper earns SRT specifically rather than dualism-in-general.
3. The Russellian-monist connection — I'd flag this as probably your strongest ally, and worth knowing. Russellian monism is the view that physics describes only structure/relations (the dispositional, the what-it-does) and is silent on the intrinsic natures (the what-it-is) of the things that bear that structure — and that consciousness (or proto-consciousness) is the intrinsic nature filling in what physics leaves as a bare relational skeleton. The search noted it's a non-epiphenomenalist view compatible with zombie-conceivability. Why it's your ally: it's already a single-domain view (one kind of stuff, with structural and intrinsic aspects), it dissolves the bridging-law problem (consciousness isn't a separate thing needing a bridge — it's the intrinsic nature of the same things physics describes structurally), and — this is the part that should interest you — it's fundamentally a claim about the relationship between *structure* (relational, objective) and *intrinsic nature* (what fills the relational role, subjective). That is extremely close to SRT's "objective = relational/structural, subjective = what occupies the role." Russellian monism might be the philosophical position your paper is reconstructing formally — physics gives you the relational graph (structure), and the intrinsic natures (the referents that fill the slots) are where the subjective lives. If so, the paper's job is partly to locate SRT as the formalization of Russellian monism, which would be a strong, defensible, and already-respected home rather than a lonely novel claim.
The honest caution for the paper (the thing I'd want a collaborator to flag): the conceivability→possibility step is genuinely where most of the field thinks the argument is vulnerable, and if SRT's motivation rests on the strong (metaphysical-possibility) reading, then SRT inherits all the controversy of that step. It might be strategically better for the paper to motivate SRT from the explanatory/representational inadequacy of structural-only ontologies (the Russellian point — physics is structurally complete but intrinsically silent, regardless of whether zombies are metaphysically possible) rather than from the full zombie modal argument. That gives SRT a motivation that doesn't depend on winning the most-contested step in philosophy of mind — it depends only on the much-more-defensible claim that structural description leaves intrinsic nature unspecified, which even many physicalists grant. The zombie is the dramatic version; the structure/intrinsic-nature gap is the robust version, and it points at single-domain-with-the-subjective-as-intrinsic-filler more directly than the zombie does.
So if it's useful: the dependency the paper needs to discharge isn't "prove materialism false" (zombie does that, contestably) — it's "motivate a single-domain ontology where the subjective is the intrinsic nature of the relational-structural objective, related internally rather than by external law," and the cleanest route to that is probably Russellian monism (structure vs. intrinsic nature) rather than the full zombie modal argument (conceivability→possibility), because the former gives SRT its single-domain-internal-relation shapeand avoids the field's main objection. The zombie can stay as the motivating drama; the structure/intrinsic-nature gap does the load-bearing work.

Ran cat > /mnt/user-data/outputs/The_Axioms_of_SRT__Session_Notes.md << 'DOC' # The Axioms of SRT: Notes Toward the Identity, the Correspondence, and the Shape of Inheritance This continues *The Axioms of SRT: A Working Set*. That note carried the lineage from *The Semantics of Relationships* and brought the set to six — Universality, Specification, Directionality, Uniqueness, Representation, Qualification — together with the trichotomy definition of the inheritance arrow. This note records what a session of work added to that foundation: a proof that the relational core is a role hierarchy in the established sense, an axiom for the top referent type and the identity theorem it yields, a bold reading of the inheritance arrow, an account of what it means to inherit a relationship faithfully, and the substitution rule that carries both the identity case and the symbol case. It keeps the proved separate from the proposed, and marks the work still owed. The primitive is unchanged. ``` x =t> y ``` This transpiles to `R(x, y, t)`, the only primitive. Equality is `x =eq> y`, written `x == y`. Free variables are universally closed; existential introduction is explicit. --- ## The six, briefly The working set is assumed, not restated in full. For reference while reading: ``` Universality E[r]: x =t> y =|> x =r> y Specification x => y =|> E(s: x =s> y): A[t: x =t> y]: x' =s> y' =|> x' =t> y' Directionality x =s> y =|> x =t> y =||> x =t> y !=|> x =s> y Uniqueness s == (x, y) & s == (x', y') =|> x == x' & y == y' Representation x =s> y =|> E[x', y']: s == (x', y') Qualification t -> (x, y) =|> x' !-> x | y' !-> y =|> x' !=t> y' ``` Universality posits the top relationship `r`. Specification posits, for any related pair, a most-specific relationship `(x, y)` that inherits into every relationship between the pair. Directionality forbids distinct relationships of one pair from mutually inheriting, which upgrades the most-specific from existing to unique. Uniqueness fixes a most-specific to one pair. Representation makes every relationship some pair's most-specific, closing the bijection between related pairs and relationships. Qualification disqualifies a relating when a role-occupant fails to inherit the role it must fill. The arrow `->` is the inheritance arrow, defined in the working set's trichotomy. Its base reading, the one used throughout what follows, is the relation reading: ``` s -> t := x =s> y =|> x =t> y ``` Where the implication holds for all `x` and `y`, the relationship `s` inherits into `t`: every pair that `s` relates, `t` relates. --- ## What the relational core proves about itself Three facts about the base inheritance arrow follow from the axioms, and they are worth stating because they are what the correspondence below rests on. The arrow is reflexive. `s -> s` is `x =s> y =|> x =s> y`, which holds for all `x` and `y` by logic alone. Nothing is assumed. The arrow is transitive. If `s -> t` and `t -> u`, then any pair `s` relates, `t` relates, and so `u` relates; hence `s -> u`. Again logic alone. The arrow is antisymmetric, and this is the one that uses an axiom. Suppose `s -> t` and `t -> s`. Then `s` and `t` relate exactly the same pairs. Take any pair `(a, b)` that `s` relates — and there is one, because to be a relationship at all is to occupy the relation position of some relating, so a relationship that relates nothing is not a relationship but merely a referent that never appears in the relation slot. Then `t` relates `(a, b)` as well, and Directionality applies to that shared pair: distinct relationships of one pair cannot mutually inherit. So `s == t`. ``` (E[u, v]: u =s> v) & s -> t & t -> s =|> s == t ``` The relational core is therefore a partial order on relationships — reflexive and transitive by logic, antisymmetric by Directionality — with a top from Universality, a bottom per pair from Specification, and a bijection to related pairs from Uniqueness and Representation together. There is no separate "totality" assumption needed to rule out empty relationships; the role-based nature of relationship-hood already does it. --- ## The correspondence with role hierarchies The relational core was not built in isolation, and it can be checked against an established theory rather than asserted to be new. Description logic studies *role hierarchies*: a partial order of binary relations under inclusion. The check is a map, built carefully, with both directions verified and the bounds named. Send each relationship `s` to the set of pairs it relates — its extension. Send the inheritance `s -> t` to the inclusion of the one extension in the other. Under this map: Each relationship becomes a binary relation on the referents, directly from `R`. The inheritance `s -> t` holds exactly when `s`'s extension is contained in `t`'s extension. This is immediate from the base reading: `s -> t` is `x =s> y =|> x =t> y`, which says precisely that every pair related by `s` is related by `t` — extension inclusion, in both directions. The order is already its own reflexive-transitive closure, because the base arrow is already reflexive and transitive. No two distinct relationships are equivalent, because antisymmetry forbids `s -> t` and `t -> s` with `s` and `t` distinct. So SRT's relational inheritance is the role-inclusion fragment of a role hierarchy, established under the map and not by resemblance. The notion of role-based inheritance that description logic formalized appears to be the same notion as SRT's relational inheritance, on that fragment. Two bounds are worth stating plainly. First, role hierarchies in their full form include role *composition* — the relation "related through `s`, then through `t`" — and SRT has no composition operator. This is deliberate: composition carries an existential middle that, iterated, runs to infinity, and SRT keeps composition symbolic, minting a named composite on demand rather than closing the relationship set under an operator. Second, where description logic enforces the directedness of the hierarchy by a syntactic restriction on which inclusions may be written, SRT derives it as a consequence of Directionality. Same effect, different provenance — one a restriction on the language, the other a theorem of the theory. The exercise also corrects an earlier loose claim. It is tempting to say SRT's inheritance is non-extensional where role hierarchies are extensional — that two relationships could relate the same pairs yet differ. But antisymmetry derives `s == t` from mutual inheritance, and mutual inheritance is coextension. So on the inclusion fragment, SRT and role hierarchies agree that coextensive relationships are identical. SRT's non-extensionality, where it lives, lives in the role-readings or in symbolism, not in relational inclusion. --- ## The top referent type, and the identity theorem Universality posits a top relationship. There is a parallel commitment one level over, on referents rather than relationships, and it is an axiom for the same reason Universality is: nothing prior grounds the existence of a top, so its existence must be posited. ### Identity ``` E[ref]: x -> ref & ref == (ref, ref) ``` There exists a referent `ref` that every referent inherits, and whose most-specific relationship with itself is itself. The naming recommends the interpretation: `ref` is *referent* — the type every referent bears by being one. As `r` is the top of the relationship hierarchy, `ref` is the top of the type hierarchy. The second conjunct pins `ref` as its own most-specific, so its canonical form is `ref =ref> ref`, all three positions the same referent. From this the universal self-relation is a theorem rather than a separate commitment. ``` x =x> x ``` Every referent inherits `ref`. The canonical form of `ref` is the all-equal form. To inherit `ref` is to bear its form, and the most-specific way to bear the all-equal form at `x`, short of being `ref` itself, is `x =x> x`. So the self-relation falls out of inheriting the top type. We had treated `x =x> x` as carrying axiomatic weight; it is a consequence of every referent being a referent. ### Why the self-relation matters Read the canonical form of the top type under two names for the one referent. ``` ref =ref> ref eq =eq> eq ``` The first says everything is a referent, including the one that represents referent-hood. The second says everything is equal to itself, including the one that represents equality. They are the same statement about the same all-equal form. Following the chain for any referent `x`: ``` x -> ref x =x> x x =ref> x ``` Inheriting `ref` gives the all-equal self-relation `x =x> x`, and bearing that inherited form is `x =ref> x`. So "`x` is a referent" — the type-label `x =ref> x` — is the same statement as "`x` equals itself" — `x =x> x`. To label every referent as a referent is to say every referent is equal to itself. This is not imposed; it falls out of the top type's form being all-equal. Equality is not added as a separate primitive `=`; it is what the universal type-label already is. The step from `x =x> x` to `x =ref> x` is licensed by form, not by substituting equals. Inheriting the all-equal canonical form simply is having one's own all-equal self-relation. There is no appeal to logical identity hidden in the move; the route runs through the inherited form. ### One referent, two names `ref` and `eq` are the same referent, or synonyms for it should we choose to formalize that identification. But the role each plays conditions the name we want. `ref` is type-like, specific to the domain — the type of being a thing here — and it is not the right handle for *comparison*. `eq` is relationship-like, general — the relating that holds between things that are the same — and it is not the right handle for *type-comprehension*. They coincide because the all-equal form is at once the universal type-label and self-equality. The single referent underneath, named differently in different roles, is the first clean instance of a general fact the theory keeps meeting: a referent may need different names in different roles, even when it is one referent. The role indexes the name; the referent is single. --- ## The inheritance arrow as self-relation The arrow `->` has had its base reading as relation-inclusion. There is a bolder reading that unifies it with the self-relation. ``` x -> t := x =t> x ``` To inherit `t` is to bear `t` as a self-relation. This collapses three things classical systems keep apart — that `x` has property `t`, that `x` is of type `t`, and that `x` inherits `t` — into one statement. The property arrow and the inheritance arrow become the same arrow, and `x =y> x` reads, for any `y`, as `x` inheriting `y`. The boldness is in the right place. The all-equal self-relation is a form at which several general rules degenerate to the same thing, which is why `x =x> x`, `ref`, and `eq` keep arriving from different directions: the all-equal form is over-determined, and every general rule evaluated there gives the same self-relation. This is also where redundancy hides. The rule that inheriting `t` yields `x =t> x` turns out to be the relation reading of inheritance evaluated at the self-relation — one rule wearing the appearance of two. Finding such coincidences is how the axiom set is kept minimal. --- ## Inheriting a relationship faithfully If one relationship is to be derived from another — if `x' =t'> y'` is to be a faithful specialization of `x =t> y` — what is required? The naive demand, that `x' =t'> y'` imply `x' =t> y'`, asks too little. It follows from `t' -> t` alone, by the relation reading at the occupants `x'` and `y'`. That is only substitutability of the relation. The real requirement is that the child preserve the structure of the parent: every inheritance that holds among the three positions of the parent must hold among the three positions of the child. All three positions specialize, the relation among them. ``` x =t> y x' -> x t' -> t y' -> y ``` with the cross-position conditions ``` x -> y =|> x' -> y' y -> x =|> y' -> x' x -> t =|> x' -> t' t -> x =|> t' -> x' y -> t =|> y' -> t' t -> y =|> t' -> y' ``` A valid specialization of `Manager =supervises> Employee`, in a setting where a manager is an employee, is `SeniorManager =mentorsThroughManagerialCoaching> Manager`. The subject specializes, the object specializes, and the relation specializes — supervising becomes a more specific supervising. The relation position is not a fixed operator carried down unchanged; it is a third position that specializes like the others. Leaving it inert is the habit of treating the relationship as a function applied to arguments, and it is the wrong habit here. The structure being preserved is the inheritance pattern among the three positions, read through inheritance rather than raw identity. Two positions are the same when they mutually inherit, ordered when one inherits the other, independent when neither does. The governing asymmetry is that different may generalize to same, but same may not specialize to different — identifications may be added going up, never removed going down. So the more general form is the more identified, and the more specific is the more distinct. The all-equal form `x =x> x` is the top; the generic form with all three positions distinct lies below it. Two consequences follow from the asymmetry rather than being stipulated. A property — the form with subject and object identified — is a kind of relationship, but no relationship derives from a property, because that would split the subject-object identification going down, which is forbidden. And one only makes symbols from symbols, by the same monotonicity: symbol structure, once present, is preserved downward and cannot be introduced where the parent lacked it. Finding the pattern is recursive: to know the form of `x =t> y` one needs the inheritance relations among `x`, `t`, `y`, which depend on the relationships they participate in, and so on. The recursion terminates, because at each step only the relationships that actually apply are consulted — a finite catalogue — and Directionality makes the inheritance graph acyclic. A finite acyclic graph bottoms out at the literals and self-relations. Becoming more specific is descending this graph by accumulating applicable relationships, and the recursion that finds them measures how specific a thing is. The structure does not compose freely, and this is correct. If the parent has a cross-position edge into a position that is then further specialized — if `y'` inherits `x'`, and `x'` is refined to `x''` with `x'' -> x'` — preserving the edge requires `y' -> x''`, which does not follow from `x'' -> x'`. Inheritance does not run backward down a specialization. So inheriting a relationship is transitive only when specialization does not orphan an incoming cross-position edge. Whether such an orphaned edge should break the inheritance or be re-established downward is a design question, not yet settled. --- ## The substitution rule, and where symbolization enters Inheriting through specification gives substitution into the relation position, at any form. The self-symbolizing form has the subject and relation identified and the object distinct. ``` symbol =symbol> literal x =x> y x =symbol> y ``` Specializing the occupants of the first to `x` and `y` gives `x =x> y`, and the relation reading then puts `symbol` into the relation position, giving `x =symbol> y`. The same rule, at the all-equal form, gives the identity result. ``` ref =ref> ref x =x> x x =ref> x ``` These are one substitution rule at two forms. The `ref` case is the maximally collapsed corner, all three positions equal; the `symbol` case keeps the object distinct and never collapses. So the type-label result is the degenerate instance, and the symbol case is the general one — the generality runs opposite to how it first appears. The symbol case cannot be synthesized from the type-label case, because the type-label case is what is left only when the object also collapses into the subject. This is where symbolization enters the type system, and it enters because generalization forces it. Specializing — going down — substitutes a concrete more-specific referent, preserves the structure, needs no symbol, and is always available. Generalizing — going up — cannot place a bare type into a relatum position, because a type-label is not a relatum. It must place a *symbol* for "some X," a referent that inherits X and stands for an arbitrary one of its inheritors. Two ways to write "an employee" present themselves. The first puts the existential in the position directly: ``` (e -> Employee) e -> Employee (e -> Employee) =symbol> e ``` Here `e` is introduced existentially by the act of making the symbol; the symbol compiles to something existential, but it is named, and can be reasoned about symbolically. The second lifts the whole relationship to symbols and keeps the existential inside the symbol's own definition, so the relationship graph stays a graph of definite edges: ``` (SeniorManager) =(supervises)> (SomeEmployee) E[e]: (SomeEmployee) =(SomeEmployee)> e -> Manager ``` Now the graph carries only definite edges between symbol nodes; the abstraction lives as a node with an existential definition, not as an existential edge. Everything stays describable by a relationship graph. The symbol `(SomeEmployee)` is the most-specific generalization of its type, and that is what a class is. A type points symbolically down to its instances; a class structurally characterizes their collection. In SRT they are one node, because the symbol is itself a referent in the graph — pointing down and being the upper bound coincide. Symbols enter the inheritance hierarchy as nodes. The upper structure of the hierarchy is symbolic, built by generalizing; the lower structure is the concrete referents, the literal floor. Classes are free, made going up; instances are earned, found going down. The asymmetry that keeps this honest: missing a symbol is fine, because symbols are made freely; missing a thing is a real problem, because a referent cannot be wished into existence and the descent to a concrete witness can fail. But generalization is self-witnessing — one generalizes from a specific thing, so the witness is already in hand. Talking abstractly is therefore always safe; bringing an abstraction down to a new concrete witness is where it can fail. Symbolization adds symbols, never things. Reference outruns realization: one can speak of far more than one can point to, and that is the ordinary condition of language, not a defect of the theory. This is also the resolution of the question Gödel raises. The tradition after Gödel extends a theory by reflection, preserving consistency, and pays for it with an unbounded ordinal climb — a transfinite patching of holes. SRT extends by symbolization, preserving semantics through symbolism, and stays finite. The incompleteness was never a hole. It is the ordinary fact that one has not named everything, and one mints a symbol on finding a thing worth studying. Read correctly, the patch is not an axiom but a new symbol pointing at a new thing — which is what reference is. --- ## What is owed The substitution behavior of `x =ref> x` and `x =symbol> y` is not yet a finished axiomatization, and it should not become one large block of conditions. Propositional logic can be given a single axiom; it should not be. The elegant statement of a theory names the few things that generate the rest. The work still owed: The role-indexed reading of `->` needs to be pinned, so that the inheritance of a referent in one position by a referent in another is well-typed. The structure-preservation conditions and the reconciliation of the two tops both presuppose it. The relationship `r -> ref` is the forcing case: false under the relation reading, true under the referent reading, so a single unindexed arrow cannot carry both without asserting a falsehood. The cross-position conditions need to be resolved — whether they are independent, whether pairwise preservation is complete or higher conditions are needed, and how they behave under composition. They do not compose freely; transitivity fails when specialization orphans an incoming edge, and the choice between breaking the inheritance and re-establishing the edge downward is open. The type side needs its own most-specific. A referent under several incomparable types has no canonical type, where a pair under several relationships has a canonical relating by Specification. Either a most-specific-type axiom is added, the type-side echo of Specification, or multiple maximal types are tolerated and the default arrow is allowed to be set-valued. Symbolization needs its axiom as the up-direction — the minimal generator for "some X," the form of the symbol node, and the precise content of the act that adds a symbol when reference requires it. And sets need to be reached, through how unspecific things relate to all possible substitutions. Until that goes through, no claim about unifying mathematics is earned. --- ## What this note establishes, and what it does not The relational core is the load-bearing part. The six axioms, the three facts about the base arrow, and the correspondence with role hierarchies are proved or checked. The Identity axiom and the theorem `x =x> x` are a clean addition in the same register. Everything from the bold reading onward — the self-relation arrow, the structure-preservation account, the substitution rule — is strong proposal rather than locked axiom, and a reader should not mistake the steadiness of the prose for the status of the claims. The honest soft spot is that the role-indexed arrow, which the working set introduced and this note relies on, is not yet pinned, and several of the cleaner statements here — the reconciliation of `r` and `ref`, the cross-position conditions — are conditional on a definition still to be written. The identification of `ref` and `eq` as one referent is a choice flagged but not made. And the claim that the all-equal form and the generic form sit at opposite poles of a single ordering is stated more confidently than the enumeration of forms yet supports; whether the orderings invert across the whole range or only meet at the poles is open. What the note does is keep the proved apart from the proposed, record the corrections the work forced — that no totality axiom is needed, that the inclusion fragment is not where non-extensionality lives, that the type-label case is the degenerate one and not the general one, that the attribute rule is derivable — and resist the single-block axiomatization while saying clearly what is still owed. It is written this way on purpose. The theory advances by realization, and the realizations overturn earlier forms — a most-specific that was first a term and then a witness, an inheritance arrow that was read three ways before one was kept, an extension claim made and then refuted by its own proof. Preserving the phases is not bookkeeping. The forms we abandoned are where the errors live, and a reader who does not see them abandoned will re-derive them. So each phase records what was believed, what broke it, and what replaced it. The current edge of the theory is the last phase, and it is open. The primitive has been stable throughout. ``` x =t> y ``` This transpiles to `R(x, y, t)`, the only primitive of the theory: `x` relates to `y` through `t`. Equality is `x =eq> y`, written `x == y`. Free variables in an axiom are universally closed; existential introduction is explicit. --- ## Phase I — The relational core The first stable achievement is a set of axioms governing relationships and their inheritance. It carries the lineage of *The Semantics of Relationships*, which named three — Universality, Specification, Directionality — and showed the most-specific relationship `(x, y)` falling out of them. The set then grew to six. ``` Universality E[r]: x =t> y =|> x =r> y Specification x => y =|> E(s: x =s> y): A[t: x =t> y]: x' =s> y' =|> x' =t> y' Directionality x =s> y =|> x =t> y =||> x =t> y !=|> x =s> y Uniqueness s == (x, y) & s == (x', y') =|> x == x' & y == y' Representation x =s> y =|> E[x', y']: s == (x', y') ``` Universality posits a top relationship `r`: every relationship between two referents is also a relationship through `r`. The naming recommends the interpretation — `r` is *relationship*. Specification posits, for any related pair, a most-specific relationship that inherits into every relationship between the pair. The witness is restricted — `E(s: x =s> y)` posits an `s` that actually relates `x` and `y`, so the relating is a condition on what exists rather than an antecedent that could be satisfied vacuously. Directionality forbids distinct relationships of one pair from mutually inheriting. This is what makes inheritance directed, and it upgrades Specification's most-specific from existing to unique: two rival most-specifics for the same pair would each inherit the other, which Directionality forbids unless they are the same. Uniqueness fixes a most-specific to one pair — the dual of Directionality, which fixes a pair and collapses rival relationships. Uniqueness fixes a relationship and collapses rival pairs. Representation makes every relationship some pair's most-specific. With Specification giving each pair a unique bottom and Uniqueness making distinct pairs have distinct bottoms, Representation closes a bijection between related pairs and relationships. Its single existential is irreducible — it is the one axiom that posits rather than collapses. The base reading of the inheritance arrow is relation-inclusion. ``` s -> t := x =s> y =|> x =t> y ``` Where this holds for all `x` and `y`, `s` inherits into `t`: every pair `s` relates, `t` relates. Three facts follow. The arrow is reflexive and transitive by logic alone. It is antisymmetric by Directionality: if `s -> t` and `t -> s`, the two relate the same pairs, and any shared pair lets Directionality force `s == t`. ``` (E[u, v]: u =s> v) & s -> t & t -> s =|> s == t ``` So the relational core is a partial order on relationships, with a top from Universality, a bottom per pair from Specification, and a bijection to related pairs from Uniqueness and Representation. **A realization within this phase, worth preserving because it corrects a tempting error.** The antisymmetry proof needs a shared pair, which raised the worry that a relationship relating *nothing* would escape it — two such would inherit each other vacuously, and a "totality" axiom seemed needed to forbid them. The worry is misplaced. To be a relationship is to occupy the relation position of some relating; a thing that relates nothing is not a relationship that fails to relate, but a referent that simply never appears in the relation slot. So the shared-pair hypothesis is automatic, and no totality axiom is needed. The empty relationship is not a gap to be closed but a non-case. --- ## Phase II — Qualification, and the trichotomy of the arrow The sixth axiom concerns when a relating can fail. ``` Qualification t -> (x, y) =|> x' !-> x | y' !-> y =|> x' !=t> y' ``` If `t` inherits the most-specific `(x, y)`, and either `x'` fails to inherit `x` or `y'` fails to inherit `y`, then `x'` does not relate to `y'` through `t`. Read as types: a relationship type is a signature `t(x:X, y:Y)`, and failing the inheritance condition at a role-occupant disqualifies the relating. Types say what could be true; they do not generate truth. Qualification uses the arrow at positions the base reading does not cover — subject (`x' !-> x`) and object (`y' !-> y`). This forced the question of what `->` means off the relation position, and the answer was a trichotomy: any `T' -> T` resolves, off one shared configuration, into exactly one of three role-pairings — relation, subject, or object. ``` T' -> T := E[x, x', y, y', t]: x =(x, y)> y & x' =t> y' =|> ( T' == t & T == (x, y) ) | ( T' == x' & T == x ) | ( T' == y' & T == y ) ``` One configuration, one inheritance notion, read from whichever position the referents occupy. This is the definition Qualification requires — it can disqualify on the failure of the subject- or object-pairing only because those pairings are defined here. **The realization that opens the next phase.** This trichotomy is stated, but it is not yet *pinned* in a way that makes cross-position inheritance well-typed on its own, and later phases lean on it heavily — the reconciliation of the two tops and the structure-preservation conditions both read inheritance across positions. The single arrow carrying three readings becomes a pressure point, and the relationship `r -> ref` (Phase IV) is where the pressure shows: it is false under the relation reading and true under the referent reading, so one unindexed arrow cannot carry both without asserting a falsehood. Pinning the role-indexed arrow is the largest piece of work the theory currently owes. --- ## Phase III — Confirming the relational core against role hierarchies Before building further, the relational core was checked against an established theory rather than assumed novel. Description logic studies role hierarchies — partial orders of binary relations under inclusion. The check is a map, built with both directions verified and the bounds named. Send each relationship to the set of pairs it relates, its extension. Send `s -> t` to the inclusion of `s`'s extension in `t`'s. Under this map: each relationship is a binary relation, from `R` directly; `s -> t` holds exactly when `s`'s extension is contained in `t`'s, immediately from the base reading; the order is its own reflexive-transitive closure, because the base arrow is already reflexive and transitive; and no two distinct relationships are equivalent, by antisymmetry. So SRT's relational inheritance is the role-inclusion fragment of a role hierarchy, established under the map. The role-based inheritance description logic formalized appears to be the same notion as SRT's relational inheritance, on that fragment. The bounds are real. Role hierarchies in full include role *composition* — "related through `s`, then `t`" — and SRT has no composition operator, deliberately: composition carries an existential middle that, iterated, runs to infinity, so SRT keeps composition symbolic, minting a named composite on demand rather than closing the relationship set under an operator. And where description logic enforces directedness by a syntactic restriction on the language, SRT derives it from Directionality — same effect, a theorem rather than a restriction. **The correction this phase forced.** It had been loosely said that SRT's inheritance is non-extensional where role hierarchies are extensional — that two relationships might relate the same pairs yet differ. The antisymmetry proof refutes this: mutual inheritance is coextension, and it derives `s == t`. So on the inclusion fragment SRT and role hierarchies *agree* that coextensive relationships are identical. SRT's non-extensionality, where it lives, lives in the role-readings or in symbolism — not in relational inclusion. The map corrected a claim that had been asserted from intuition. --- ## Phase IV — The top referent type, and identity Universality gives a top relationship. The parallel commitment one level over, on referents, is an axiom for the same reason: nothing prior grounds the existence of a top, so it must be posited. ``` Identity E[ref]: x -> ref & ref == (ref, ref) ``` There exists a referent `ref` that every referent inherits, whose most-specific relationship with itself is itself. The naming recommends the interpretation — `ref` is *referent*, the type every referent bears by being one. As `r` tops the relationship hierarchy, `ref` tops the type hierarchy. The second conjunct pins `ref` as its own most-specific, so its canonical form is `ref =ref> ref`, all three positions the same referent. From this the universal self-relation is a theorem. ``` x =x> x ``` Every referent inherits `ref`; the canonical form of `ref` is all-equal; to inherit `ref` is to bear that form, and the most-specific way to bear it at `x`, short of being `ref`, is `x =x> x`. The self-relation, which had been treated as carrying axiomatic weight, is a consequence of every referent being a referent. The reason this matters. Read the top type's canonical form under two names for the one referent. ``` ref =ref> ref eq =eq> eq ``` The first says everything is a referent, including the one representing referent-hood; the second says everything equals itself, including the one representing equality. They are the same statement about the same all-equal form. For any referent: ``` x -> ref x =x> x x =ref> x ``` So "`x` is a referent," the type-label `x =ref> x`, is the same statement as "`x` equals itself," `x =x> x`. Labeling every referent a referent is saying every referent equals itself. Equality is not added as a separate primitive; it is what the universal type-label already is. The step from `x =x> x` to `x =ref> x` is licensed by form, not by substituting equals — inheriting the all-equal canonical form simply is having one's own all-equal self-relation. **A structural realization recorded here.** `ref` and `eq` are the same referent, or synonyms for it should we formalize the identification. But the role conditions the name. `ref` is type-like, the type of being a thing here, and is wrong for *comparison*. `eq` is relationship-like, the relating between things that are the same, and is wrong for *type-comprehension*. They coincide because the all-equal form is at once the universal type-label and self-equality. This is the first clean instance of a fact the theory keeps meeting: a referent may need different names in different roles, even when it is one referent. The role indexes the name; the referent is single. This realization is what makes pinning the role-indexed arrow (Phase II's debt) not merely a technical fix but a step the theory's own content demands. --- ## Phase V — Inheritance as the self-relation A bolder reading of the arrow emerged, unifying it with the self-relation. ``` x -> t := x =t> x ``` To inherit `t` is to bear `t` as a self-relation. This collapses three things classical systems keep apart — that `x` has property `t`, that `x` is of type `t`, that `x` inherits `t` — into one statement. The property arrow and the inheritance arrow become one, and `x =y> x` reads, for any `y`, as `x` inheriting `y`. The boldness sits where it should. The all-equal self-relation is a form at which several general rules degenerate to the same thing, which is why `x =x> x`, `ref`, and `eq` keep arriving from different directions — the form is over-determined. This is where redundancy hides, and finding it minimizes the axioms. **The realization, and a correction of the order of generality.** It first appeared that the type-label case was fundamental and everything else a special case of it. The opposite is true, and the symbol case shows it. Inheriting through specification gives substitution into the relation position at *any* form. ``` symbol =symbol> literal x =x> y x =symbol> y ``` Specializing the occupants of `symbol =symbol> literal` to `x` and `y` gives `x =x> y`, and the relation reading puts `symbol` into the relation position, giving `x =symbol> y`. The same rule, at the all-equal form, gives the identity result of Phase IV. ``` ref =ref> ref x =x> x x =ref> x ``` These are one substitution rule at two forms. The `ref` case is the maximally collapsed corner, all three positions equal; the `symbol` case keeps the object distinct and never collapses. So the type-label result is the *degenerate* instance, and the symbol case is the general one. The symbol case cannot be synthesized from the type-label case — the type-label case is only what remains when the object collapses into the subject too. The generality runs opposite to how it first appeared, and the correction is the content of this phase. --- ## Phase VI — What it is to inherit a relationship If `x' =t'> y'` is to be a faithful specialization of `x =t> y`, what is required? This phase records both a wrong answer and the right one. **The wrong answer, preserved because it is tempting.** That `x' =t'> y'` should imply `x' =t> y'`. This asks too little — it follows from `t' -> t` alone, by the relation reading at the occupants. It is only substitutability of the relation, not faithful specialization. A second wrong turn, also preserved: a competing definition of subject-inheritance as a *universal* condition ("`x'` carries every relationship `x` carries") was invented and then withdrawn, because inventing a parallel formalism to justify the existing one is no justification — the theory already has its definition in the Phase II trichotomy, and the task is to work from it, not to replace it. **The right answer.** The child must preserve the structure of the parent: every inheritance holding among the three positions of the parent must hold among the three of the child, and all three positions specialize — the relation among them. ``` x =t> y x' -> x t' -> t y' -> y ``` with the cross-position conditions ``` x -> y =|> x' -> y' y -> x =|> y' -> x' x -> t =|> x' -> t' t -> x =|> t' -> x' y -> t =|> y' -> t' t -> y =|> t' -> y' ``` A valid specialization of `Manager =supervises> Employee`, where a manager is an employee, is `SeniorManager =mentorsThroughManagerialCoaching> Manager`: subject, object, and relation all specialize, supervising becoming a more specific supervising. The relation position is not a fixed operator carried down unchanged; it is a third position specializing like the others. Treating it as inert is the habit of reading the relationship as a function applied to arguments, and it is the wrong habit. The structure preserved is the inheritance pattern among the positions, read through inheritance rather than raw identity: two positions are the same when they mutually inherit, ordered when one inherits the other, independent when neither does. The governing asymmetry is that different may generalize to same but same may not specialize to different — identifications may be added going up, never removed going down. So the more general form is the more identified, the more specific the more distinct. The all-equal form is the top; the form with all three positions distinct lies below. Two consequences follow from the asymmetry rather than being stipulated. A property — subject and object identified — is a kind of relationship, but no relationship derives from a property, since that would split the identification going down. And one makes symbols only from symbols, by the same monotonicity. Finding the pattern is recursive: the form of `x =t> y` needs the inheritance among `x`, `t`, `y`, which needs the relationships they participate in, and so on. It terminates, because only the relationships that actually apply are consulted — a finite catalogue — and Directionality makes the inheritance graph acyclic, bottoming out at literals and self-relations. Becoming more specific is descending this graph by accumulating applicable relationships, and the recursion that finds them measures specificity. **The realization that bounds this phase.** The structure does not compose freely, and that is correct. If the parent has a cross-position edge into a position then further specialized — `y'` inherits `x'`, and `x'` is refined to `x''` with `x'' -> x'` — preserving the edge needs `y' -> x''`, which does not follow from `x'' -> x'`. Inheritance does not run backward down a specialization. So inheriting a relationship is transitive only when specialization does not orphan an incoming cross-position edge. Whether such an edge should break the inheritance or be re-established downward is unsettled. --- ## Phase VII — Symbolization as the up-direction Phase V's substitution rule places symbolization at a precise spot: generalization. Specializing — going down — substitutes a concrete more-specific referent, preserves structure, needs no symbol, and is always available. Generalizing — going up — cannot place a bare type into a relatum position, because a type-label is not a relatum. It must place a symbol for "some X," a referent that inherits X and stands for an arbitrary inheritor. Two forms for "an employee" were considered. The first puts the existential in the position: ``` (e -> Employee) e -> Employee (e -> Employee) =symbol> e ``` `e` is introduced existentially by making the symbol; it compiles to something existential but is named, and reasoned about symbolically. The second lifts the relationship to symbols and keeps the existential inside the symbol's own definition, so the graph stays one of definite edges: ``` (SeniorManager) =(supervises)> (SomeEmployee) E[e]: (SomeEmployee) =(SomeEmployee)> e -> Manager ``` The graph now carries only definite edges between symbol nodes; the abstraction is a node with an existential definition, not an existential edge. Everything stays describable by a relationship graph. `(SomeEmployee)` is the most-specific generalization of its type, and that is what a class is. A type points symbolically down to its instances; a class structurally characterizes their collection. In SRT they are one node, because the symbol is itself a referent in the graph — pointing down and being the upper bound coincide. Symbols enter the inheritance hierarchy as nodes. Its upper structure is symbolic, built by generalizing; its lower structure is the concrete referents, the literal floor. Classes are free, made going up; instances are earned, found going down. **The realization that keeps this honest, and that superseded an earlier one.** An earlier formulation had transduction fire "at the inconsistency boundary" — mint a witness whenever an existential lacked one. That is wrong, and the correction is the content here: you do not wish things into being. Missing a *symbol* is fine, because symbols are made freely. Missing a *thing* is a real problem, because a referent cannot be conjured and the descent to a concrete witness can fail or be impossible. But generalization is self-witnessing — one generalizes from a specific thing, so the witness is already in hand. Talking abstractly is always safe; bringing an abstraction down to a *new* concrete witness is where it can fail. Symbolization adds symbols, never things. Reference outruns realization: one can speak of far more than one can point to, and that is the ordinary condition of language. This is also where SRT meets Gödel. The tradition after Gödel extends a theory by reflection, preserving consistency, and pays with an unbounded ordinal climb — a transfinite patching of holes. SRT extends by symbolization, preserving semantics through symbolism, and stays finite. The incompleteness was never a hole. It is the ordinary fact that one has not named everything, and one mints a symbol on finding a thing worth studying. Read correctly, the patch is not an axiom but a new symbol pointing at a new thing — which is what reference is. Frozen as a static layer of axioms, symbolization gains nothing and the Gödel sentence reappears; kept as the act of naming a newly-found thing, there is no hole to patch. --- ## The current edge The work the theory now owes, stated so it does not collapse into one block of conditions. Propositional logic admits a single axiom; it should not be given one. The elegant statement names the few things that generate the rest. The role-indexed reading of `->` must be pinned, so that a referent in one position inheriting a referent in another is well-typed. Phase II raised the debt; Phase IV showed the theory's content demands it; Phases IV and VI both lean on it. The relationship `r -> ref` is the forcing case — false under the relation reading, true under the referent reading. The cross-position conditions of Phase VI must be resolved: whether they are independent, whether pairwise preservation is complete, and how they behave under composition. They do not compose freely; the orphaned-edge case is open between breaking the inheritance and re-establishing the edge. The type side needs its own most-specific. A referent under several incomparable types has no canonical type, where a pair under several relationships has one by Specification. Either a most-specific-type axiom is added — the type-side echo of Specification — or multiple maximal types are tolerated and the default arrow is set-valued. Symbolization needs its axiom as the up-direction — the minimal generator for "some X," the form of the symbol node, and the precise content of the act that adds a symbol when reference requires it. And sets must be reached, through how unspecific things relate to all possible substitutions. Until that goes through, no claim about unifying mathematics is earned. --- ## On this document The phases are preserved deliberately, including the wrong forms: the function-symbol most-specific that smuggled totality and was returned to the Specification witness; the invented auxiliary predicates and a non-existent equality referent that were removed; the universal subject-inheritance invented and withdrawn; the inconsistency-boundary transduction superseded by the honest dead-end; the non-extensionality claim refuted by its own proof; the order of generality corrected so the symbol case is general and the type-label case degenerate. These are not errors to be embarrassed by but the structure of the work, and a reader needs them to avoid re-deriving them. The load-bearing parts are Phases I through IV: the six axioms, the facts about the base arrow, the role-hierarchy correspondence, and the Identity axiom with its theorem. These are proved or checked. Phases V through VII are strong proposal — the self-relation arrow, the structure-preservation account, the substitution rule and symbolization. The steadiness of the prose should not be read as equal confidence across the two; the line is at the end of Phase IV. The honest soft spot remains the role-indexed arrow, which several clean statements in Phases IV and VI silently depend on and which is not yet pinned. The identification of `ref` and `eq` is flagged, not made. And the claim that the all-equal form and the generic form sit at opposite poles of one ordering is stated more confidently than the enumeration of forms yet supports — whether the orderings invert across the whole range or only meet at the poles is itself part of the current edge.
